title: 100,000 machines failing hourly is a different kind of system
body: A storage system on one machine is easy. A storage system spread over 100,000 machines, in many regions, serving thousands of teams while machines fail every hour, is a different kind of system. Scaling it comes down to three big questions: how do we split the data (partitioning, splitting, rebalancing), where do we put each piece (placement, failure domains, heat), and how do we stay fast and fair as we grow (hot spots, tenants, regions, capacity, and tail latency).
deeper:
The chapter grounds every idea in one running example: a global app with 1 billion users that stores profiles, photos and videos, messages, logs and events, and analytics data. Each of those data types stresses a different part of the system. Photos and videos pile up into exabytes of bytes. Messages create bursts of writes at peak hours. Thumbnails create trillions of tiny objects. Many internal teams (search, ads, ML) want to share the same clusters. Users on every continent want low latency, and some of them live under laws that say their data must stay in their region.

The three questions build on one another. Splitting data into shards is the basic tool, but shards must then be placed so that no single failure destroys every copy and no single disk gets too much traffic. Finally, once the system is split and placed, it must keep working as load shifts: hot items appear, tenants collide, regions add speed-of-light delays, hardware must be bought months ahead, and fan-out requests are slowed by the single slowest server. The rest of the chapter takes these problems in that order.

quiz.q: What are the three big questions behind scaling a storage system?
quiz.a: How to split the data (partitioning), where to put each piece (placement across failure domains and by heat), and how to stay fast and fair while growing (hot spots, tenants, regions, capacity, tail latency).

title: “It must scale” hides six different problems
body: Saying a system must scale hides at least six separate problems, and each breaks a different part. Capacity (total bytes) fills disks and stretches rebuild times. IOPS and throughput saturate disk heads, NICs, and storage-node CPUs. Metadata operations (opens, lists, renames, lookups) overload the metadata service, often before data nodes. Object count bloats indexes and per-object memory. Tenants create fairness, isolation, and quota problems. Regions add latency, consistency, and legal constraints. Naming which dimension is growing tells you what will break first.
deeper:
The chapter maps each dimension onto the running 1-billion-user app. Capacity: photos and videos reach exabytes, so the pain is disks filling up and rebuild times growing as drives get bigger. IOPS: message writes at peak hours hammer disk heads, network cards, and CPUs on storage nodes. Metadata operations: listing a user's photo album is a metadata operation, and the metadata service often breaks before any data node does. Object count: trillions of small thumbnails blow up index size, memory per object, and directory size even though their total bytes are modest. Tenants: search, ads, and ML all share one cluster, so the question becomes who gets what and how one team is stopped from hurting another. Regions: EU users' data must stay in the EU, and cross-continent copies bring latency and consistency trade-offs.

The practical lesson is diagnostic. When someone says a design does not scale, ask along which axis. A design that handles 10x more bytes gracefully can still collapse at 10x more objects or 10x more tenants, because a different component is on the critical path for each.

quiz.q: Why is “the system must scale” an incomplete requirement?
quiz.a: Scale has at least six dimensions (bytes, IOPS, metadata ops, object count, tenants, regions), and each one breaks a different component, so you must say which is growing.

title: Bigger drives, same head: IOPS per terabyte keeps falling
body: Bytes and operations scale separately. A 20 TB hard drive holds five times more data than a 4 TB drive, but it still has a single head arm that performs roughly the same 100 to 200 random IOPS (assuming a typical 7,200 RPM drive). So as drives grow, the IOPS available per terabyte shrinks. Cold data that is rarely read does not care. Hot data that is read often suffers badly, because far more data now competes for the same limited number of random operations.
deeper:
The mechanical reason is that a hard drive's random performance is set by seek time and rotation, not by platter density. Doubling capacity packs more bits under the same arm, but the arm still has to physically move and wait for the sector to spin around. The chapter's figure of about 100 to 200 random IOPS for a typical 7,200 RPM drive is an assumption, but the direction is what matters: IOPS per drive is roughly flat while terabytes per drive keep climbing.

This has design consequences that echo through the chapter. It is one reason placement must be heat-aware: if many hot objects land on the same big drive, that drive's small IOPS budget becomes a hot spot. It is why hyperscale object stores like S3 spread each tenant thinly across huge numbers of drives, so that no single drive sees too many hot requests. It is also why smaller systems must reserve IOPS headroom or move hot data to flash. Treating capacity planning as a bytes-only exercise will produce a cluster that has plenty of free space but cannot serve its traffic.

quiz.q: Why does buying larger hard drives make hot data perform worse per terabyte?
quiz.a: Each drive keeps one head arm with roughly the same random IOPS, so more terabytes share the same IOPS budget and IOPS per terabyte falls.

title: One billion tiny objects: 1 TB of data, a billion headaches
body: Object count matters as much as total size. One billion 1 KB objects add up to only 1 TB, which fits on one drive, but they also create one billion metadata entries. Every entry costs index space, memory, and work when listing or looking things up. Many systems hit the limit of their metadata service long before they run out of disk. HDFS is the famous example: its single metadata server ran out of room for file entries while the data nodes still had plenty of free space.
deeper:
The core insight is that many costs are per object, not per byte. Metadata entries, index memory, directory sizes, and listing work all scale with how many things you store, regardless of how small each thing is. A system that easily handles 10x more bytes can still fail at 10x more objects, because the bottleneck moves from the data plane (which scales by adding disks) to the metadata plane (which needs consistency and often lives on fewer machines).

In the running example, trillions of small thumbnails are the threat. Their total bytes are modest compared with full-size videos, yet they could dominate metadata load. The chapter points back to Chapter 2 for HDFS, whose single NameNode held all metadata in memory and became the classic cautionary tale. Later in this chapter, Meta's Tectonic shows the fix at scale: metadata lives in a sharded key-value store and is sized for object count, with a representative cluster tracking 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks. When planning, always ask for the expected object count, not just the expected petabytes.

quiz.q: Why can a system that easily handles 10x more bytes still fail at 10x more objects?
quiz.a: Many costs are per object, not per byte: metadata entries, index memory, listing work. The metadata service hits its limit long before the disks fill.

title: Sharding: the basic tool of scale
body: Partitioning, also called sharding, means splitting a dataset into smaller pieces called partitions or shards. Each shard lives on one server or one replica group. It is the basic tool of scale: if one machine cannot hold or serve all the data, split it across many machines. Every sharded system must then answer one central question: for a given key, which shard owns it? There are four main answers: range partitioning, hash partitioning, consistent hashing, and directory-based partitioning.
deeper:
The four schemes trade off along a few axes: how evenly they spread keys, whether they keep range scans cheap, how much data moves when you add or remove capacity, and how much freedom you have to put a shard wherever you like.

Range partitioning keeps sorted keys together, which makes scans cheap but invites hot spots. Hash partitioning spreads keys evenly but destroys ordering, and with a naive modulo it moves almost every key when the server count changes. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes limits movement to about 1/N of the data on a membership change. Directory-based partitioning keeps an explicit map from shard to servers, giving total freedom at the cost of a critical lookup service.

These are not mutually exclusive in practice. Many systems hash keys into a fixed number of logical shards and then use a directory to decide where each logical shard lives. Google's Slicer, for example, has applications hash keys into a large key space and then assigns ranges of that space to servers. Picking the right answer depends on your access pattern: scan-heavy workloads lean to ranges, point-lookup workloads lean to hashing.

quiz.q: What single question must every partitioning scheme answer?
quiz.a: For a given key, which shard owns it? The four main answers are range, hash, consistent hashing, and directory-based lookup.

title: Range partitioning: sorted keys, cheap scans
body: In range partitioning, each shard owns a continuous, sorted range of keys. For example, shard 1 owns user IDs from a to f, shard 2 owns f to m, and so on. A small table maps each range to its shard, and when a range grows too large it is split in two. The big advantage is that range scans are cheap: a query like all messages in this chat between time T1 and T2 touches only a few neighboring shards, because data sorted together stays together.
deeper:
Range partitioning is the model behind several well-known systems, each with its own name for a range: Bigtable calls them tablets, Spanner calls them splits, HBase calls them regions, and CockroachDB calls them ranges. The range-to-shard table is small because it only stores boundaries, not individual keys.

Splitting is natural here: pick a split key in the middle of an oversized range and create two child ranges. Merging small adjacent ranges back together is also natural, and Spanner and CockroachDB both do it. Because the boundaries are explicit, the system can adapt to data that grows unevenly without rehashing anything.

The weakness is that the distribution of load follows the distribution of keys. If keys are uniformly spread and accessed evenly, ranges balance well after a few splits. If keys are skewed, such as timestamps or auto-incrementing IDs, all activity piles onto one end of the key space. The comparison table in the chapter rates range partitioning as needing splits for even spread, supporting range scans, moving only split ranges on resize, and offering medium flexibility.

quiz.q: Why is range partitioning a good fit for queries like messages in a chat between T1 and T2?
quiz.a: Keys are stored sorted and contiguous, so a time-bounded scan touches only a few neighboring shards instead of every shard.

title: Timestamp keys turn range sharding into a one-server show
body: The main weakness of range partitioning is that sequential keys create hot spots. If keys are timestamps or increasing IDs, every new write lands in the last range, because every new key is larger than all existing keys. One server takes all the writes while the rest of the cluster sits idle. Splitting that last range does not help much either: the new top range immediately becomes the hot one. The problem lies in the key design, not in the number of shards.
deeper:
This pattern shows up again and again in the chapter. DynamoDB's paper notes that a sequentially accessed key range will not benefit from split-for-consumption, and DynamoDB detects this pattern and avoids useless splits. The chapter's common-mistake box warns that auto-splitting fixes hot ranges but cannot fix a monotonically increasing key.

The standard fixes change the key rather than the partitioning. You can prefix keys with a hash so that consecutive writes scatter across the key space, or use randomized IDs instead of counters. The trade-off is that you lose some of the cheap-scan benefit: records written close together in time are no longer stored close together. Some designs accept this for write-heavy tables and keep range order only where scans truly matter.

The general lesson is to think about the write pattern of your key before choosing range partitioning. Range order is a feature for reads that scan and a liability for writes that always append to the same end.

quiz.q: Why doesn't splitting the hot range fix a timestamp-keyed hot spot?
quiz.a: New keys always sort after existing ones, so after a split the new top range receives all the writes and becomes the hot spot again.

title: Hash partitioning: even spread, no range scans
body: In hash partitioning, the system computes hash(key) and uses the result to pick a shard. The simplest form is hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of shards. Because a good hash scrambles keys, load spreads evenly even when the real keys are sequential, so timestamps no longer create one hot shard. The cost is that range scans disappear: keys that are neighbors in sorted order end up on random shards, so a range query must ask every shard.
deeper:
Hash partitioning is the natural choice for point-lookup workloads, where requests fetch one key at a time and never ask for a sorted range. It removes the append hot spot that plagues range partitioning with timestamp keys, because consecutive timestamps hash to unrelated values.

The trade-off is sharp. Any query that needs order or a range, such as the last hour of events, now has to scatter to every shard and gather the results. That multiplies load and exposes the query to the slowest shard, a problem the chapter returns to in the tail latency section.

Hash partitioning also does nothing about a single hot key. A viral video or a celebrity profile hashes to exactly one shard no matter what hash function you pick. Even spread is a property of many keys, not of one popular key.

Finally, the plain modulo form has a serious operational flaw when the shard count changes, covered separately. That flaw is why real systems pair hashing with either fixed logical shards or consistent hashing rather than using raw hash mod N.

quiz.q: What do you gain and lose by switching from range to hash partitioning?
quiz.a: You gain even load spread even for sequential keys; you lose cheap range scans, since neighboring keys land on random shards.

title: hash mod N: add one server, move 91 percent of your data
body: Plain hash(key) mod N has a terrible property: when N changes, almost every key moves to a different shard. Going from 10 shards to 11 moves about 10/11, roughly 91 percent, of all keys, because most hash values now produce a different remainder. At petabyte scale, reshuffling nearly all data just to add one server is a disaster: it saturates the network for a long time and hurts user traffic. The chapter's comparison table labels hash mod N as fit only for simple caches, and says to avoid it.
deeper:
The math is simple. A key stays put only if hash(key) mod 10 equals hash(key) mod 11, which is true for only about 1 in 11 keys. Everything else must be copied to a new home. In a cache this is tolerable, since a miss just refetches from the source, which is why the table limits its use to simple caches. In a durable store, every moved key is real bytes on the network and disks, competing with user requests.

There are two widely used fixes. The first is to decouple keys from servers by hashing into a large, fixed number of logical shards and then assigning logical shards to servers; adding a server moves whole logical shards and never changes any key's shard. The second is consistent hashing, where adding or removing a server moves only about 1/N of the keys, those adjacent to the changed server on a hash ring.

Both fixes share the same idea: never let the physical server count appear directly in the formula that maps a key to its location.

quiz.q: With plain hash mod N, what fraction of keys move going from 10 to 11 shards, and why?
quiz.a: About 10/11 (roughly 91 percent), because changing the divisor changes the remainder for almost every hash value; only about 1 in 11 keys keeps its shard.

title: Fixed logical shards: hash once, move shards not keys
body: A common trick is to create many more logical shards than servers and never change the logical shard count. Keys are hashed into, say, 4,096 logical shards, and a separate mapping assigns logical shards to physical servers. When you add servers, you move whole logical shards to them; no key ever changes which logical shard it belongs to. Uber's Schemaless (2014 to 2016) used a fixed 4,096 logical shards on top of MySQL. Ceph does something similar with placement groups.
deeper:
This approach combines the even spread of hashing with cheap growth. The key-to-shard function is fixed forever, so there is never a mass reshuffle of individual keys. Only the shard-to-server mapping changes, and it changes in coarse, whole-shard units that are easy to copy, verify, and switch over.

The number of logical shards is a long-term commitment. It must be large enough that each server can hold several shards, so load can be balanced by moving individual shards, and so the system can grow to many more servers without a shard becoming larger than one server can handle. Uber chose 4,096 for Schemaless. Ceph's placement groups play the same role: objects hash into a fixed pg_num of groups per pool, and the CRUSH algorithm places groups, not objects, onto disks (Ceph's autoscaler can adjust pg_num as a pool grows).

The comparison table in the chapter rates this scheme as evenly spread, without range scans, moving whole shards only on resize, with medium flexibility, and lists Schemaless, Ceph PGs, and Vitess as users.

quiz.q: How do fixed logical shards avoid the mod-N reshuffle problem?
quiz.a: The key-to-logical-shard mapping never changes; adding servers only moves whole logical shards between machines, so individual keys are never remapped.

title: Consistent hashing: a ring where only 1/N of data moves
body: Consistent hashing fixes the almost-every-key-moves problem. Picture a ring of hash values from 0 to 2^64. Each server is placed at a point on the ring by hashing its name. Each key is hashed onto the same ring and belongs to the next server clockwise. When a server joins, it takes keys only from its one neighbor. When a server leaves, only its keys move, to its neighbor. On average only 1/N of the data moves when membership changes.
deeper:
The chapter's diagram shows the full lookup path. Take the key for user 42, hash it to a point on the ring, and walk clockwise to the next virtual node, say vnode A-17, which belongs to server A. Server A holds the primary replica. For more replicas, keep walking clockwise and pick the next distinct physical servers, B and then C, skipping any further vnodes that belong to A. This ensures the replicas land on different machines.

The key property is locality of change. Because each server owns only the arc just before its position, adding a server splits one arc, and removing a server merges its arc into the next. Nothing else on the ring is disturbed. Compare that with hash mod N, where changing N remaps almost everything.

In the chapter's comparison table, consistent hashing with virtual nodes gives even spread, no range scans, about 1/N data moved on resize, and medium flexibility. Its limitation is that ownership is dictated by hash positions, so you cannot freely place a particular shard by load, hardware type, or region.

quiz.q: When a server joins a consistent hashing ring, where does its data come from?
quiz.a: Only from its clockwise neighbor, whose arc it splits. Everything else stays put, so on average only about 1/N of data moves.

title: Virtual nodes: fix a lumpy ring with many small arcs
body: With only a few servers, the random points on a consistent hashing ring are uneven: one server might own 30 percent of the ring and another only 5 percent. The fix is virtual nodes, or vnodes. Each physical server is placed at many points on the ring, for example 100 to 256. Now every server owns many small arcs scattered around the ring, and the total ownership comes out close to even. Vnodes also let a bigger machine own more arcs than a smaller one.
deeper:
The statistics are straightforward: a few random points cut a circle into very unequal pieces, but the sum of many random pieces per server averages out. With 100 to 256 vnodes per server, the variance in ownership drops enough that no server is badly overloaded.

Vnodes bring two extra benefits. First, heterogeneous hardware becomes easy: give a machine with twice the capacity twice as many vnodes, and it takes twice the share of keys. Second, when a server leaves, its many small arcs are absorbed by many different neighbors instead of dumping all its load on one unlucky successor. The same is true in reverse when a server joins: it takes a little from many servers rather than a lot from one.

When choosing replicas, a vnode-based system must walk past vnodes that belong to a physical server it has already chosen, so that replicas land on distinct machines. That detail, shown in the chapter's ring diagram, is easy to get wrong and would silently put two copies on one server.

quiz.q: Why do consistent hashing systems place each server at 100 to 256 points on the ring?
quiz.a: A few random points split the ring unevenly; many small arcs per server average out to near-even ownership and let bigger machines take more arcs.

title: Dynamo made the ring famous; Discord uses it to coalesce
body: Amazon's Dynamo paper (SOSP 2007) made consistent hashing with virtual nodes famous, and Cassandra, Riak, and many caches adopted the design. It lets any node compute where a key lives and keeps data movement small when nodes join or leave. Discord offers a modern twist: its Rust data service routes requests with consistent hashing by channel ID, so all requests for the same channel land on the same instance. That instance can then merge identical concurrent requests into one database query.
deeper:
Dynamo's contribution was showing that a large key-value store could be built with no central directory: every node knows the ring, so any node can route any request. The design influenced a generation of systems, notably Cassandra and Riak. The same paper is also known for keeping conflicting versions and letting the application merge them, which the chapter revisits in the multi-region section.

Discord's use is instructive because it treats consistent hashing as a routing tool, not only a storage layout. By sending every request for a given channel to the same service instance, Discord creates a single place where duplicate in-flight requests can be detected. If thousands of users open a busy channel at the same moment, the instance issues one query to the database and fans the result out to all waiters. This request coalescing is one of the chapter's answers to the single-hot-key problem, where splitting shards cannot help.

The limitation of pure consistent hashing, as the next sections show, is that it cannot place data by load, fault domain, or region on demand.

quiz.q: Why does Discord route requests by channel ID with consistent hashing?
quiz.a: So all requests for the same channel reach the same instance, which can coalesce identical concurrent requests into one database query.

title: Directory partitioning: put any shard anywhere
body: In directory-based, or lookup-based, partitioning, a separate service stores an explicit map, such as shard 1234 lives on servers X, Y, and Z. Clients ask the directory or cache its answers. The upside is total freedom: you can move any shard anywhere for any reason, including load, hardware type, failure domain, region, or cost, because no hash function dictates the mapping. The downside is that the directory becomes a critical dependency. It must be highly available, and clients must cope with stale maps.
deeper:
This is the model used by Google Slicer, Meta Shard Manager, LinkedIn Helix, and the placement layer of most large blob stores. Its flexibility is exactly what large operators need: they want to put a shard near its users, keep replicas in separate fault domains, give a hot shard to a lightly loaded machine, and drain a server before upgrading it. A hash function cannot express those choices.

The cost is operational. If the directory is down, clients that do not have a cached map cannot find data, so the directory must be replicated and highly available. Clients also cache the map for speed, which means they will sometimes send a request to a server that no longer owns the shard. The system needs a way to reject and redirect those requests, and the move protocol must fence writes during ownership changes so two servers never both think they own a shard.

In the chapter's comparison table, directory partitioning is rated as controlled spread, range scans depending on design, moving only what you choose on resize, and high flexibility.

quiz.q: What is the main price you pay for the flexibility of directory-based partitioning?
quiz.a: The directory becomes a critical dependency that must be highly available, and clients must handle stale cached maps that point to the wrong server.

title: Five ways to shard, compared side by side
body: The chapter compares five schemes. Range: needs splits for even spread, supports range scans, moves only split ranges on resize, medium flexibility (Bigtable, Spanner, HBase, CockroachDB). Hash mod N: even spread, no scans, moves almost everything on resize, low flexibility (simple caches only, avoid). Hash into fixed logical shards: even, no scans, whole shards move, medium (Schemaless, Ceph PGs, Vitess). Consistent hashing with vnodes: even, no scans, about 1/N moves, medium (Dynamo, Cassandra). Directory: controlled spread, scans depend, move only what you choose, high flexibility (Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix).
deeper:
Reading the table by column helps decisions. If you need range scans, range partitioning is the only scheme with a clear yes; directory-based systems can support scans only if their shards are ranges. If you need even spread without thinking, any hash-based scheme delivers it, but range partitioning needs active splitting.

The data-moved-on-resize column separates good from bad designs most sharply. Hash mod N moves almost everything and should be avoided outside simple caches. Fixed logical shards and consistent hashing both keep movement small, in different ways: one moves whole logical shards, the other about 1/N of keys. Directory-based systems move exactly what the operator or controller decides.

The flexibility column explains the industry trend covered next. Google, Meta, and LinkedIn all needed to place shards by load, fault domain, hardware, and region, and to drain servers before upgrades. Only the directory model offers high flexibility, so all three built central, directory-style shard managers, often layered on top of hashing into a large key space.

quiz.q: Which partitioning scheme should you avoid for durable storage, and why?
quiz.a: Hash mod N: changing the shard count remaps almost every key, forcing a near-total data reshuffle. The table limits it to simple caches.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
title: Why Google, Meta, and LinkedIn built generic shard managers
body: Every sharded system needs the same hard features: assign shards to servers, move them when servers die, balance load, and avoid dropping requests while shards move. Getting these right is difficult, and having every team rebuild them wastes effort and multiplies bugs. So large companies built generic shard managers: shared services that handle assignment, movement, and balancing for many applications at once. The three published examples are Google Slicer, Meta Shard Manager, and LinkedIn Helix.
deeper:
The chapter's In industry box summarizes the pattern: Google (Slicer, 2016), Meta (Shard Manager, 2020 to 2021), and LinkedIn (Helix, 2012) all chose a central, directory-style shard manager over pure consistent hashing. The reason was control. They needed to place shards by load, fault domain, and region, and to drain servers gracefully before upgrades. Consistent hashing fixes placement by hash position, which cannot express those goals.

A generic shard manager also concentrates expertise. Handoff protocols, rate-limited moves, fencing during ownership changes, and failure detection are subtle, and one well-tested implementation serving hundreds of applications is more reliable than hundreds of partial ones. Meta's Shard Manager, for example, accounts for about 54 percent of sharded applications at Facebook.

The trade-off is that the shard manager becomes shared critical infrastructure. Its data plane, which routes requests, must be fast and highly available, while its control plane, which decides assignments, can be slower and off the request path. Slicer made that split its central design idea.

quiz.q: Why did Google, Meta, and LinkedIn pick directory-style shard managers over pure consistent hashing?
quiz.a: They needed to place shards by load, fault domain, and region, and to drain servers before upgrades, which a hash ring cannot express.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
title: Slicer: split the fast data plane from the smart control plane
body: Slicer (OSDI 2016) is Google's general-purpose auto-sharding service. Its key idea is separation. A data plane forwards each request to the right server, fast and reliably. A control plane watches load and server health and decides the assignment of work to servers, entirely off the request path. Applications hash their keys into a large key space. Slicer divides that space into ranges called slices and assigns slices to servers, so requests never wait on the slow, thoughtful balancing decisions.
deeper:
Separating the planes lets each be optimized for its job. The data plane only needs a current assignment table and must be quick and highly available, because every request passes through it. The control plane can gather load statistics, run balancing logic, and take its time, because a slightly delayed rebalancing decision does not slow any individual request.

The slice design combines hashing with a directory. Hashing keys into a large key space gives even distribution and hides skew in real keys. Assigning contiguous ranges of that hashed space, the slices, to servers gives the control plane something coarse to move. Slicer can then react to load in several ways: give a hot slice more replicas, split a slice that is too busy, or merge slices that are cold, all while trying to limit churn, meaning it avoids moving too much at once.

Limiting churn matters because every move costs network bandwidth and risks a brief disruption. A balancer that chases every small fluctuation would spend more resources moving data than it saves, the same concern behind the chapter's warning about naive rebalancing.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of Slicer keeping its control plane off the request path?
quiz.a: Slow balancing decisions never delay requests; the data plane just routes with the current assignment, fast and reliable, while the control plane rebalances in the background.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
title: Slicer's real win: median workload used 63% fewer resources
body: The Slicer paper reports serving 2 to 7 million requests per second in production. The more important number is that the median Slicer-managed workload used 63 percent fewer resources than it would have with static sharding. The reason is that static sharding wastes capacity: every shard must be provisioned for its own peak, even though shards peak at different times. A dynamic sharder can move and replicate slices to follow load, so the fleet is sized for the combined load, not the sum of peaks.
deeper:
This is the economic argument for auto-sharding. In a static scheme, each shard gets a fixed server, and that server must handle its shard's worst moment. Across hundreds of shards, most servers are idle most of the time, waiting for a peak that happens occasionally. The total fleet equals the sum of every shard's peak.

With dynamic assignment, the control plane watches load and reacts: it splits a slice that is becoming hot, adds replicas to share read load, merges cold slices, and moves work onto less busy servers. The fleet only needs to cover the actual combined load plus some headroom. That difference, for the median workload, was 63 percent fewer resources.

The same idea reappears elsewhere in the chapter. DynamoDB moved from fixed per-partition throughput to table-level admission control and split-for-consumption because per-partition limits wasted capacity and throttled customers. S3 spreads tenants across millions of drives so bursts cancel out. Tectonic shares spare IOPS across tenants. In each case, flexibility in where load goes lets a system provision for aggregate demand rather than for every piece's worst case.

quiz.q: Why does static sharding waste capacity compared with Slicer-style dynamic sharding?
quiz.a: Each static shard must be provisioned for its own peak; dynamic sharding moves and replicates slices to follow load, so the fleet is sized for combined demand.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
title: Meta Shard Manager: tens of millions of shards, 1M+ machines
body: Meta's Shard Manager does the same job as Slicer at Meta. A 2020 blog post said it managed tens of millions of shards on hundreds of thousands of servers across hundreds of applications. The SOSP 2021 paper says it runs on over one million machines and accounts for about 54 percent of sharded applications at Facebook. Applications declare placement constraints, such as spread replicas across fault domains or keep a shard near its users, and Shard Manager balances multiple resources, including CPU, memory, and storage.
deeper:
Shard Manager treats placement as a constrained optimization problem. Each application states what it needs, and the system searches for an assignment that respects fault-domain spread, locality to users, and resource limits across several dimensions at once. Balancing only one resource, such as shard count, would leave some machines out of memory while others run out of CPU.

The paper is candid about a practical limit: a full constraint solver is too slow for near-real-time placement at global scale. When a server fails or load shifts, the system must respond in seconds, not hours. So practical systems use faster heuristics that find good-enough assignments quickly, rather than a perfect optimum too late.

The paper's first big observation also shapes the design: most applications need geo-distribution. A shard manager that only places within one cluster is not enough; it must place shards across regions, which ties shard management to the multi-region topics later in the chapter, such as leader placement and data residency.

quiz.q: Why do practical shard managers like Meta's use heuristics instead of a full constraint solver?
quiz.a: A full solver is too slow for near-real-time placement at global scale; heuristics find good-enough assignments fast enough to react to failures and load changes.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
title: Planned events outnumber unplanned failures about 1,000 to 1
body: Meta's Shard Manager paper made an observation that matters for all of storage: planned events, such as software upgrades, happen about 1,000 times more often than unplanned failures. So the most important feature of a shard manager is not recovering from a crash. It is moving shards and handing off primaries gracefully before a planned restart. If a system only handles failures well, every routine deploy looks like a failure to clients, which means constant small outages.
deeper:
The arithmetic behind this is intuitive once stated. A large fleet deploys new software frequently, and each deploy restarts many servers. Hardware crashes are comparatively rare. If each restart drops the shards on that server until clients time out and failover kicks in, the planned events dominate unavailability.

The better approach is to treat a planned restart as an opportunity to prepare. Before the process stops, the shard manager moves its shards elsewhere or promotes a replica on another server to primary, and only then lets the restart proceed. Clients see a clean handoff instead of errors and retries. This is also why rolling restarts appear as a feature in systems like LinkedIn's Venice, which uses Helix.

The chapter notes that it returns to this topic in Chapter 9 on operations. For design reviews, the takeaway is to ask not only how the system recovers from a crash but how it drains and hands off before a planned event, because that path runs about 1,000 times more often.

quiz.q: Why did Meta's Shard Manager paper emphasize planned events over failures?
quiz.a: Planned events like upgrades happen about 1,000 times more often than unplanned failures, so graceful shard moves and primary handoff before restarts matter more for availability than crash recovery.

section: 8.3 Shard management services: Slicer, Shard Manager, Helix
title: Helix: state machines for every replica
body: LinkedIn built Apache Helix, described at SoCC 2012 as a generic cluster management framework for partitioned, replicated resources. Helix models each replica with a state machine, for example OFFLINE, SLAVE, and MASTER, and computes the transitions needed when nodes join, fail, or restart. Instead of writing ad hoc failover code, an application defines its states and allowed transitions, and Helix orchestrates them across the cluster. LinkedIn's derived-data store Venice uses Helix for replica placement, rack awareness, rebalancing, and rolling restarts.
deeper:
Modeling replicas as state machines gives cluster management a precise vocabulary. Every replica is in a known state, and every change, such as promoting a replica to MASTER after the old one fails or taking a replica OFFLINE before a restart, is an explicit transition. Helix computes the target state of the whole cluster and issues the transitions required to reach it, respecting constraints such as at most one MASTER per partition.

Venice shows the range of features this enables. Partition-replica placement decides which nodes hold which replicas. Rack-aware placement ensures copies of the same partition are not all in one rack, a failure-domain rule covered later in the chapter. Automatic rebalancing on failure moves replicas when nodes die. Rolling restarts let the cluster upgrade node by node without losing availability, which ties directly to Meta's observation that planned events vastly outnumber failures.

Helix is the oldest of the three shard managers in the chapter, dating to 2012, and along with Slicer and Shard Manager it represents the industry's convergence on central, directory-style cluster management.

quiz.q: How does Helix decide what to do when a node joins, fails, or restarts?
quiz.a: Each replica has a state machine (such as OFFLINE, SLAVE, MASTER); Helix computes the state transitions needed to reach a valid target cluster state and orchestrates them.

title: Splitting and merging: reshape shards while serving traffic
body: Data does not grow evenly. Some shards get big, some get hot, and some become nearly empty, so a scalable system must change its partitioning while still serving traffic. Splitting turns one shard into two; for range partitioning, you pick a split key and create two child ranges. The new child can start on the same server, so no data moves at first, and be moved later. Merging is the reverse: combining small adjacent shards to cut per-shard overhead.
deeper:
Starting a new child on the same server is a useful trick. A split then becomes a cheap metadata change: the boundaries are recorded, and both children keep serving from the same machine. Moving one child elsewhere is a separate, rate-limited rebalancing step that can happen when convenient. This keeps splits fast, which matters when a shard is becoming hot and needs relief quickly.

Merging addresses the opposite problem. After many deletes, a system can be left with lots of tiny shards. Each shard carries fixed overhead regardless of its size: memory for bookkeeping, open file handles, and in consensus-based systems a Raft group with its own leader election and heartbeats. Thousands of nearly empty shards waste real resources. Spanner and CockroachDB both merge small adjacent ranges back together.

Both operations rely on range partitioning's explicit boundaries. In hash-based schemes with fixed logical shards, the equivalent move is reassigning whole logical shards among servers, since the shard boundaries themselves never change.

quiz.q: Why might a system merge shards instead of just leaving small ones alone?
quiz.a: Each shard has fixed overhead (memory, file handles, a Raft group), so many tiny shards left after deletes waste resources; Spanner and CockroachDB merge small adjacent ranges.

title: Moving a live shard in four steps
body: Rebalancing moves shards between servers so each server carries a fair load. A shard move usually works in four steps. First, copy a snapshot of the shard to the new server. Second, stream new writes, the log, to the new server until it catches up. Third, briefly pause or fence writes, switch ownership in the directory, and resume. Fourth, delete the old copy after a safety delay. This keeps the shard available throughout, with only a tiny write pause at the switch.
deeper:
Each step has a purpose. The snapshot copies the bulk of the data while the old server keeps serving normally. Because writes continue during the copy, the snapshot is immediately stale, so the log stream replays new writes on the destination until it is nearly current. The fence in step three is the critical moment: writes are paused or rejected very briefly so that no write lands on the old owner after the new owner takes over. Ownership is switched in the directory, clients are redirected, and writes resume.

The safety delay in step four protects against mistakes. If the new copy turns out to be incomplete or the new server fails right away, the old copy is still there. Deleting it immediately would turn a routine move into potential data loss.

The same pattern underlies graceful handoff before planned restarts, which Meta found to be about 1,000 times more common than crashes, and DynamoDB's autoadmin moving replicas off overloaded storage nodes. Clients with stale cached maps must be able to get a redirect rather than an error.

quiz.q: Why fence writes briefly during the ownership switch when moving a shard?
quiz.a: So no write lands on the old owner after the new owner takes over; otherwise writes could be lost or diverge between two servers that both think they own the shard.

title: Common mistake: treating rebalancing as free
body: A common mistake is treating rebalancing as free. Moving a shard copies real bytes over the network and reads and writes real disks. A naive balancer that sees a newly added, empty rack and fills it immediately can saturate the network for hours, starving user requests of bandwidth and pushing up latency across the cluster. The fix is to cap the move rate and watch user latency while moves run, so balancing happens gradually in the background instead of as a self-inflicted outage.
deeper:
Rebalancing competes with user traffic for the same resources: network links, disk heads, and CPU on storage nodes. When a new rack arrives, a greedy balancer sees a huge imbalance and tries to fix it all at once, launching many parallel copies. On hard drives with limited IOPS, and across shared top-of-rack and cluster links, that burst can dominate the hardware.

The chapter repeats the same discipline in several places. Slicer tries to limit churn, avoiding moving too much at once. The capacity planning section lists rate-limited rebalancing as a requirement for adding new racks continuously: new capacity must be filled gradually. Background work such as compaction, scrubbing, and rebalancing is also a named cause of tail latency, which is why Tectonic schedules background work in a lower TrafficClass.

In practice this means a move-rate limit, per-node limits on concurrent moves, and a feedback signal from user-facing latency. If latency climbs, the balancer slows down. The goal is not the fastest possible convergence but reaching balance without users noticing.

quiz.q: Why can adding a new empty rack hurt user latency?
quiz.a: A naive balancer rushes to fill it, launching massive data copies that saturate network and disks for hours. Cap the move rate and watch user latency.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: Failure domains: three copies in one server protect almost nothing
body: Partitioning decides which piece; placement decides which disks hold that piece's copies. Placement's main goal is that one failure never destroys all copies. A failure domain is a set of components that can fail together: a disk, a server, a rack (sharing a top-of-rack switch and power), a row, a power zone, a building, an availability zone, a region. Copies must spread across failure domains. Three copies on three disks in one server give almost no protection; three racks survive a rack failure; three zones survive a zone outage.
deeper:
The hierarchy of failure domains goes from small and frequent to large and rare. Disks fail most often, but a whole server can die from a bad power supply or motherboard, taking every disk inside with it. A rack shares a top-of-rack switch and power feed, so a switch or power failure takes out every server in it. Larger units, such as rows, power zones, buildings, availability zones, and regions, fail less often but take more with them.

Replicas and erasure-coded fragments must both follow this rule. The protection you get is set by the smallest failure domain that contains all copies. Three copies in three zones survive a zone outage, but if all three zones share a region, a regional disaster still loses everything, which is why some data is also replicated across regions.

Placement systems encode failure domains explicitly. Ceph's CRUSH uses a cluster map tree like root, datacenter, rack, host, disk, with rules such as pick three different racks. LinkedIn's Venice uses Helix for rack-aware placement, and Meta's Shard Manager lets applications ask to spread replicas across fault domains.

quiz.q: Why do three replicas on three disks in the same server give almost no protection?
quiz.a: The server is a failure domain: one power supply or motherboard failure takes all three disks at once. Copies must span separate failure domains like racks or zones.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: RS(10,4) math: why many systems erasure-code inside a datacenter
body: A Reed-Solomon RS(10,4) stripe splits data into 10 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments, 14 in total, and survives the loss of any 4. To survive a full rack failure, no rack may hold more than 4 of the 14 fragments, so you need at least 4 racks, arranged 4+4+4+2. Surviving a whole zone loss would likewise need at least 4 zones. That is why many systems use erasure coding inside a datacenter and full replication across regions.
deeper:
This back-of-envelope calculation turns the failure-domain rule into a concrete layout constraint. With RS(10,4), losing any 4 fragments is fine, but losing 5 is data loss. If one rack held 5 fragments, a single rack failure would destroy the stripe. Capping each rack at 4 fragments means 14 fragments need ceil(14/4) = 4 racks, laid out as 4, 4, 4, and 2.

The same logic applied to zones is expensive. Spreading one stripe over at least 4 zones means every read that needs 10 fragments must pull most of them across zone links, and every repair after a failure moves data between zones. Racks inside one datacenter share fast, cheap networking, so erasure coding works well there. Across regions, the network is slower and costlier, and a regional read needs data locally.

The common result is a two-level design: erasure coding within a datacenter for cheap durability against disk, server, and rack failures, and full replicas in other regions for regional disasters and local reads. Erasure coding also reappears as a tail-latency tool, since requesting extra fragments lets a reader ignore slow disks.

quiz.q: With RS(10,4), why do you need at least 4 racks to survive a rack failure?
quiz.a: The stripe tolerates losing only 4 of 14 fragments, so no rack may hold more than 4; 14 fragments at 4 per rack needs at least 4 racks (4+4+4+2).

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: CRUSH: compute where data lives instead of looking it up
body: Ceph's CRUSH (Controlled Replication Under Scalable Hashing, 2006) is a placement algorithm that computes data locations instead of looking them up in a table. The paper calls it a scalable pseudo-random data distribution function that maps data objects to storage devices without relying on a central directory, and distributes data according to user-defined policies that enforce separation of replicas across failure domains. Because every client holds the same cluster map, every client computes the same answer, with no central lookup on the read path.
deeper:
CRUSH sits between pure hashing and a directory. Like hashing, it is a deterministic function, so any client can find data without asking a server, which removes the directory as a bottleneck and single point of failure on reads. Unlike a plain hash, its input includes a description of the physical cluster and a policy, so the output respects failure domains.

The cluster map is a weighted tree, such as root, datacenter, rack, host, disk. Weights let bigger disks receive proportionally more data, which is what makes heterogeneous hardware work; the capacity planning section cites CRUSH weights as the model for mixing disk sizes during continuous add-and-retire.

When a disk is added, CRUSH moves only a proportional share of placement groups to it rather than reshuffling everything, similar in spirit to consistent hashing. The trade-off compared with a directory is flexibility: placement follows the function and the map, rather than from a free, per-group choice made for load reasons. The chapter's takeaways contrast this: CRUSH computes placement from map and rules, while directory placement is more flexible and can be heat-aware.

quiz.q: Why does CRUSH not need a central directory on the read path?
quiz.a: Every client has the same cluster map and rules, and CRUSH is deterministic, so every client computes the same list of disks for a placement group by itself.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: Object to PG to OSD: Ceph's two-step placement
body: Ceph places data in two steps. First, object to placement group: hash the object name and map it to one of pg_num placement groups (PGs) in the pool, where a PG is a bucket of many objects. Second, placement group to OSDs: CRUSH takes the PG ID, the cluster map (a tree like root, datacenter, rack, host, disk, with weights), and a rule, such as pick 3 different racks, then 1 disk in each. It outputs the list of OSDs, meaning disks, that store that PG.
deeper:
The chapter's diagram walks through one object. Its name is hashed, and hash(name) mod pg_num selects placement group 7.3a. CRUSH is then called with three inputs: the PG ID, the cluster map of root, racks, hosts, disks, and weights, and a rule of 3 replicas in different racks. The output is OSD 12 in rack 1, OSD 88 in rack 4, and OSD 203 in rack 7, so the three copies land in three separate failure domains.

Note the hash mod pg_num in step one. This is exactly the fixed-logical-shards pattern: pg_num is the fixed logical count, and objects map to PGs by a simple function. Growth is handled in step two, where CRUSH remaps PGs onto the changing set of disks. Only whole PGs move when disks are added or removed.

The rule language is what enforces failure-domain separation. Changing the rule, for example to pick 3 different datacenters, changes the protection level without changing how objects map to PGs.

quiz.q: What are Ceph's two mapping steps from object to disk?
quiz.a: The object name is hashed to one of pg_num placement groups; then CRUSH maps the PG to a set of OSDs using the cluster map and a placement rule.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: Placement groups: track thousands of groups, not millions of objects
body: Why place placement groups instead of individual objects? Tracking millions of objects one by one, each with its own location and replication state, is too costly. PGs group many objects so the system tracks and peers a manageable number of groups. Ceph's docs say mon_target_pg_per_osd defaults to 100 PGs per disk and recommend about 200, warning that values above 500 can cause excessive peering traffic and memory use. An autoscaler can change pg_num as the pool grows.
deeper:
Peering is the process where the OSDs holding a PG agree on its current state, for example after a disk restarts. It happens per PG, so the number of PGs directly sets the coordination overhead. Too few PGs per disk and data spreads unevenly, since each PG is a coarse chunk, and recovery after a failure involves few disks working in parallel. Too many PGs and every OSD spends memory and network on bookkeeping and peering chatter, which is why Ceph warns against going above 500 per OSD.

The defaults reflect this balance: target 100, recommended about 200. Because the right pg_num depends on how many OSDs a pool spans and how much data it holds, Ceph provides an autoscaler that adjusts pg_num as the pool grows, rather than requiring operators to guess once and live with it forever.

The general lesson matches the chapter's theme about counting objects, not only bytes: any per-item cost at scale must be amortized by grouping items into larger units that the control plane can manage.

quiz.q: Why does Ceph place placement groups instead of individual objects?
quiz.a: Tracking and peering millions of objects individually is too costly; PGs group objects so the system manages hundreds of groups per disk instead.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: Heat: S3 can spread one customer's workload over a million disks
body: Placement for durability is only half the job; the other half is heat. In Andy Warfield's 2023 description of Amazon S3, heat means the number of requests hitting a given disk at any point in time. Bad placement lets many hot objects land on one drive and create a hot spot. S3 deliberately puts different objects onto different sets of drives so that each customer's accesses spread over a very large number of disks. A single customer workload might be served by over a million disks.
deeper:
Heat-aware placement follows from the IOPS-per-terabyte problem earlier in the chapter. Big hard drives have few random IOPS relative to their capacity. If an unlucky placement puts several hot objects on the same drive, that drive's small IOPS budget is exhausted and requests queue, even though the fleet as a whole has plenty of spare capacity.

S3 avoids this by making placement a load-spreading tool. Rather than keeping a customer's objects together, it deliberately scatters them across different drive sets. The result is that each customer touches a vast number of disks, and each disk carries a thin slice of many customers' traffic. When one customer gets busy, the extra load is divided among so many drives that no single drive is pushed over the edge.

This suits a directory-style placement layer that can decide freely where each object goes. The chapter's takeaways note that directory-based placement is more flexible than computed placement and can be heat-aware, whereas a fixed function like CRUSH optimizes for failure-domain separation and even capacity.

quiz.q: What does heat mean in S3's placement design, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: Heat is the number of requests hitting a disk at a given time; if hot objects cluster on one drive, its limited IOPS become a hot spot despite fleet-wide spare capacity.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: At huge scale, bursts cancel out
body: Warfield's key insight about S3 is aggregation. Individual workloads are very bursty, but once you aggregate enough of them, it becomes difficult or impossible for any single workload to influence the combined peak. At huge scale, independent bursts tend to cancel out: while one customer spikes, others are quiet. Because each drive serves a thin slice of very many customers, drive-level demand becomes smooth and predictable. This is an advantage small clusters simply do not have, since they serve too few workloads for bursts to average away.
deeper:
The statistics resemble insurance. One household's claims are unpredictable, but the claims of millions of households are stable. Likewise, a single tenant's request rate might spike sharply and without warning, yet the sum across a huge population of independent tenants barely moves.

S3 turns this into engineering by combining two things: enormous scale, with a single customer workload possibly touching over a million disks, and deliberate spreading, so every disk mixes traffic from many unrelated customers. The spreading ensures each disk sees the aggregate, not any individual workload. The aggregate is smooth, so disks can run closer to their limits without frequent overload.

The same principle explains why Slicer saves resources over static sharding and why multi-tenancy saves money in general: one team's idle capacity serves another team's peak. The catch, emphasized in the chapter's senior staff lens, is that this benefit depends on scale. A cluster with a handful of large tenants will see their bursts add up rather than cancel, so it must reserve explicit headroom instead.

quiz.q: Why can a hyperscale object store tolerate very bursty individual customers?
quiz.a: Spreading each customer over huge numbers of drives means each drive sees the aggregate of many independent workloads, whose bursts cancel out, so no single workload moves the peak.

section: 8.5 Data placement: CRUSH, placement groups, and failure domains
title: Senior staff lens: cheap slow drives work only at huge scale
body: Heat-aware placement is why a hyperscale object store can use big, slow, cheap hard drives. Each drive offers few IOPS, but spreading every tenant thinly across millions of drives means no single drive receives too many hot requests. When you design a smaller system, you do not get this for free. Without millions of drives and countless independent tenants, bursts do not cancel out. You must instead reserve IOPS headroom on your drives or put hot data on flash.
deeper:
This lens is a warning against copying hyperscaler architecture without its scale. A design review might see that S3 runs on dense hard drives and conclude that a smaller internal object store can do the same. The economics that make this work, very low IOPS per terabyte offset by statistical smoothing across a huge fleet, do not transfer to a cluster of a few hundred drives with a few dozen tenants.

In a smaller system, one tenant's burst can land on a noticeable fraction of the drives, and a few simultaneous bursts can overload them. The two remedies named in the chapter each cost money in a different way. Reserving IOPS headroom means buying more drives than capacity alone would require, so you pay for spindles you keep idle. Using flash for hot data means paying more per terabyte for media with far more IOPS, and adding tiering logic to decide what is hot.

The honest design question is which of these you are paying for, and whether your capacity model counts IOPS as well as bytes, per the chapter's first lesson that bytes and operations scale separately.

quiz.q: Why can't a small storage cluster copy S3's strategy of cheap, slow hard drives for hot data?
quiz.a: It lacks the scale for bursts to cancel out across millions of drives, so it must reserve IOPS headroom or place hot data on flash.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: Hot spots: celebrities, viral videos, and timestamp keys
body: A hot spot, or hot partition, is a shard that receives much more traffic than others. Common causes include a celebrity profile that millions of people view, a viral video, a sequential key such as a timestamp where every new write hits the same end, a big customer whose traffic dwarfs everyone else's, and a batch job scanning one range. Hot spots matter because a system's capacity is only as good as its busiest shard: one overloaded server can throttle or slow requests while the rest of the cluster sits idle.
deeper:
The causes fall into distinct types that need different fixes, which is the thread running through the rest of this section. A hot range, where many different keys in one range are busy, can be fixed by splitting the range so the load divides between two servers. A single hot key, like one celebrity's profile or one viral video, cannot be split; it needs caching, read replicas, request coalescing, or key salting. A sequential key pattern, like timestamps, just moves the hot spot to the newest range after each split; it needs a different key design.

A big customer and a batch job are really multi-tenancy problems. They are handled by admission control, quotas, and priority classes, as in DynamoDB's table-level token buckets and Tectonic's traffic classes.

Detecting hot spots requires per-shard monitoring of consumed throughput and, ideally, a histogram of which keys inside the shard are busy. DynamoDB's design uses exactly that signal to decide whether a split will help and where to split. Knowing which type of hot spot you have is the first step to picking the right defense.

quiz.q: Why can't one fix handle every kind of hot spot?
quiz.a: Hot ranges can be split, but a single hot key cannot be divided and sequential keys just move the hot end; each type needs a different defense.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: DynamoDB step 1: static splits and throughput dilution
body: Early DynamoDB divided a table's provisioned throughput evenly across partitions. The paper's example: if one partition can hold at most 1,000 write capacity units (WCUs) and a table has 3,200 WCUs, DynamoDB created four partitions of 800 WCUs each. This assumed uniform access, but real workloads are uneven over time and key ranges. Two problems appeared: hot partitions, where traffic keeps hitting a few items, and throughput dilution. Customers were throttled even when their table's total capacity was high enough.
deeper:
DynamoDB's 2022 USENIX ATC paper is one of the best public accounts of hot-spot handling, because it shows the design evolving step by step, with each step fixing the previous step's failure.

Throughput dilution is the subtle problem. When a partition grew too large and was split for size, its throughput was split as well. If most traffic went to one half, that hot half now had only half the capacity it had before the split, even though nothing about the customer's workload or total provisioned capacity had changed. Growth in data made the hot keys slower.

The root cause was enforcing limits at the partition level. The paper quotes that application workloads frequently have non-uniform access patterns both over time and over key ranges. Dividing a table's capacity evenly means any partition carrying more than its share is throttled, while capacity assigned to cold partitions goes unused. The customer sees throttling errors while paying for enough throughput overall, the same kind of waste that static sharding causes, as Slicer's paper showed.

quiz.q: What is throughput dilution in early DynamoDB?
quiz.a: Splitting a partition for size also split its throughput, so a hot half received less capacity than before the split and got throttled despite ample table capacity.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: DynamoDB step 2: bursting and adaptive capacity
body: DynamoDB's first fixes were bursting and adaptive capacity. Bursting let a partition use unused capacity saved from up to the last 300 seconds, provided the storage node also had spare capacity. This absorbed short spikes. Adaptive capacity watched for long-lived skew and boosted the throughput of partitions that stayed hot. Both helped, but both had limits: they were reactive, responding only after skew had already appeared, and they were still tied to per-partition limits, so the underlying design flaw remained.
deeper:
Bursting treats unused capacity like a savings account. If a partition was quiet for a while, it banked its unused throughput for up to 300 seconds and could spend it during a short spike. The condition that the storage node also have spare capacity matters: bursting borrows from the physical machine, so it cannot promise capacity the node does not have.

Adaptive capacity targeted the other failure pattern, where a partition stays hot for a long time. It detected sustained skew and raised the hot partition's limit. That reduced throttling for stable hot spots.

The chapter's diagnosis is that both mechanisms were reactive and still tied to per-partition limits. Because the enforcement unit was still the partition, a hot partition had to be noticed and boosted after the fact, and customers could still see throttling before the system reacted. The next step changed the enforcement unit itself, moving limits from partitions to tables. Bursting's effect of packing nodes beyond their provisioned totals also created the need for step 5, balancing consumed capacity across storage nodes.

quiz.q: Why were bursting and adaptive capacity not a complete fix for DynamoDB hot partitions?
quiz.a: Both were reactive, responding only after skew appeared, and still tied to per-partition limits, so the flawed enforcement unit remained.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: DynamoDB step 3: global admission control
body: DynamoDB replaced adaptive capacity with global admission control (GAC), a service that tracks token buckets at the table level. Request routers keep local token buckets and refill them from GAC every few seconds. Now the throughput limit is enforced for the table as a whole, not per partition, so a hot partition can use the table's unused capacity from cold partitions. Partition-level token buckets remain as defense in depth, preventing any one partition from overwhelming a storage node.
deeper:
A token bucket is a simple rate limiter: tokens refill at a fixed rate, each request takes a token, and an empty bucket means reject or delay. GAC applies this at the right level. The customer pays for table throughput, so the table is what gets limited. Traffic can shift freely among partitions as long as the table total stays within budget, which directly cures throughput dilution.

The distributed design keeps it fast. Checking a central service on every request would add latency and create a bottleneck, so request routers hold local buckets and replenish them from GAC every few seconds. Most requests are admitted locally, and GAC only coordinates the totals.

Keeping partition-level buckets is important in a multi-tenant service. Storage nodes host thousands of replicas from unrelated customers, and DynamoDB caps partition-level buckets to ensure one application does not consume all or a significant share of a node's resources. GAC gives a customer flexibility across its partitions; the partition caps protect everyone else on the same hardware. GAC alone still cannot help when a single partition needs more than one node can provide, which step 4 addresses.

quiz.q: How did global admission control fix throughput dilution?
quiz.a: It enforces limits at the table level via router token buckets refilled from GAC, so a hot partition can use unused table capacity instead of a fixed per-partition share.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: DynamoDB step 4: split for consumption, not just size
body: Even with table-level limits, one partition can need more throughput than one storage node can deliver. So DynamoDB splits partitions based on consumed throughput. Once a partition's consumed throughput crosses a threshold, it is split for consumption, and the split point is chosen from the key distribution the partition has observed, so the load, not just the data, divides between the children. Splits usually complete in minutes. DynamoDB also detects cases where splitting cannot help, a single hot item or a sequential key range, and avoids those useless splits.
deeper:
The chapter's flowchart shows the logic. Monitor each partition's consumed throughput and a key histogram. If traffic is below the split threshold, keep monitoring. If above, check whether the traffic is on a single key or a sequential range. If yes, do not split; rely on admission control and caching. If no, choose a split point from the observed key distribution, create two child partitions, and move a child to a less loaded node if needed.

Choosing the split point from observed traffic is what distinguishes this from a size split. A size split picks the middle of the data; a consumption split picks the point that divides the requests evenly, which may be far from the data midpoint.

The exclusions are principled. Splitting divides a key range between two partitions, but one key cannot be divided, so a single hot item would remain entirely in one child. A sequential pattern, where all traffic hits the newest keys, just moves the hot end into whichever child holds the top of the range. Splitting in those cases wastes work and adds partitions without relieving load.

quiz.q: Why does split-for-consumption not help with a single hot item or a sequential key pattern?
quiz.a: One key cannot be divided, so it stays in one child; a sequential pattern just moves the hot end to the new child. Caching, replicas, or key design are needed.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: DynamoDB step 5: rebalance the nodes, not just the partitions
body: Once partitions could burst and share table-level capacity, DynamoDB's storage nodes ended up packed beyond their provisioned totals: the sum of what their replicas might use could exceed what the node could deliver. So each storage node monitors the throughput its replicas actually consume. When a node crosses a threshold, an autoadmin service moves some replicas to other nodes. This balances consumed capacity across the fleet, so flexible per-partition usage does not overload any single machine.
deeper:
This step closes the loop created by the earlier ones. Static per-partition limits had one virtue: a node's worst-case load was known, because every partition had a hard cap. Bursting and table-level admission control removed that certainty, letting individual partitions use more than their original share. That flexibility is good for customers but means a node can be oversubscribed if several of its partitions spike at once.

Rather than going back to rigid limits, DynamoDB accepted overbooking and added active balancing. Nodes watch real consumption, and when one runs hot, the autoadmin service moves some of its replicas to other nodes.

The overall arc of DynamoDB's evolution, from static partition limits to bursting, then table-level admission control, split-for-consumption, and consumption-based balancing, mirrors the chapter's broader lesson. Per-partition limits cause throttling under skew. Table-level admission control plus split-for-consumption fixes most skew, and balancing keeps nodes healthy, but none of it fixes a single hot key.

quiz.q: Why did DynamoDB need to rebalance replicas based on consumed capacity?
quiz.a: Bursting and table-level limits let partitions exceed their old shares, so nodes became packed beyond provisioned totals; moving replicas off hot nodes prevents overload.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: You can't split a key: four defenses for one hot item
body: Splitting cannot help when a single key is hot, because you cannot split a key. The common answers: caching in front, such as memcache or a CDN for photos, which is the main defense for reads. Read replicas of the hot shard; Slicer can assign more replicas to hot slices. Request coalescing: Discord's Rust data service merges identical concurrent requests so the database sees one query instead of thousands. And for writes, key salting, which spreads one hot key across several sub-keys.
deeper:
Each defense targets a different shape of load. Caching removes reads from the storage system entirely. A viral photo served from a CDN never reaches the storage node, which is why it is the main read defense. Read replicas spread the remaining reads across several servers holding the same data; Slicer's ability to give a hot slice more replicas is an automated form of this.

Request coalescing attacks duplication. When thousands of clients ask for the same thing at the same moment, most of those requests are redundant. Discord routes by channel ID with consistent hashing so that all requests for one channel reach the same instance, which can then merge identical in-flight requests into a single database query and share the result.

Writes are the hardest case, because caches and read replicas do nothing for them. Key salting, covered next, handles hot counters by spreading writes. In DynamoDB's flowchart, the no-split path for a single hot key explicitly says to rely on admission control and caching, which matches this list.

quiz.q: Why is caching the main defense against a single hot key for reads?
quiz.a: Splitting cannot divide one key, but a cache or CDN serves repeated reads before they reach storage, removing the load entirely.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: Key salting: split a hot counter into 16 sub-keys
body: Key salting handles a single hot key under heavy writes. Instead of one counter such as likes:video123, the application writes to N sub-keys, for example likes:video123:0 through likes:video123:15, choosing one at random or by rotation for each increment. The sub-keys hash to different shards, so the writes spread across many servers. To read the total, the application reads all sub-keys and sums them. The cost is that the application must know about the salting; the database will not do it automatically.
deeper:
Salting turns one hot key into many lukewarm ones. With 16 sub-keys, each shard sees roughly one sixteenth of the write load, and the hot spot disappears as long as 16 servers can carry the total.

The trade-offs are real. Reads become more expensive: a single logical read now fans out to N sub-keys, which multiplies read work and exposes the read to the slowest of N responses, the tail latency effect discussed at the end of the chapter. Salting therefore suits write-heavy, read-light data such as like counters, view counts, or event tallies. It is a poor fit for data that is read constantly.

The application complexity is the other cost. Every writer and reader must use the same scheme and the same N, and changing N later requires care. Sums across sub-keys are also not atomic snapshots unless extra coordination is added.

The broader principle from the chapter's common-mistake box is to design keys so that writes spread, using a hash prefix or randomized IDs, and to cache hot reads, rather than hoping the database will fix hot keys by itself.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off of salting a hot counter into N sub-keys?
quiz.a: Writes spread across N shards, removing the hot spot, but every read must fetch and sum all N sub-keys, and the application must implement the scheme.

section: 8.6 Hot spots: detecting and splitting them
title: Common mistake: “the database auto-splits, so we're fine”
body: A common mistake is assuming the database auto-splits, so hot spots are solved. Auto-split fixes hot ranges, where many keys in one range are busy. It does not fix a single hot key, because one key cannot be divided. It also cannot fix a monotonically increasing key, such as a timestamp, because every split just leaves the newest range hot. The fix is design, not hope: shape keys so writes spread, using a hash prefix or randomized IDs, and cache hot reads.
deeper:
This mistake is common because auto-splitting is a real and useful feature, and database documentation rightly advertises it. DynamoDB's split-for-consumption handles hot ranges well, with splits usually completing in minutes, and range-partitioned systems such as Bigtable, Spanner, and CockroachDB split ranges automatically. It is easy to generalize that into a belief that the database handles all hot spots.

DynamoDB's own paper spells out the limits: a single hot item or a sequentially accessed key range will not benefit from splitting, and DynamoDB detects these patterns and deliberately avoids useless splits. In other words, even the most advanced auto-splitter explicitly gives up on these two cases.

The responsibility therefore lands on schema and key design. For write patterns, avoid monotonically increasing keys as the leading part of the key, prefixing a hash or using random IDs instead. For hot individual items, plan caching, read replicas, request coalescing, or key salting from the start. In a design review, ask which keys could become hot, such as a celebrity, a viral item, or the current time bucket, and what happens when they do.

quiz.q: Why doesn't database auto-splitting solve every hot spot?
quiz.a: It only fixes hot ranges. A single hot key cannot be divided, and monotonically increasing keys keep the newest range hot after each split.

title: Metadata belongs in a sharded database, not one server's RAM
body: The data plane scales by adding disks, but the metadata plane is harder: it needs consistency, and its access is skewed toward popular files and directories. Two lessons follow. First, put metadata in a scalable database, not in one server's memory: Google's Colossus stores metadata in Bigtable, and Meta's Tectonic stores it in ZippyDB, a sharded key-value store. Second, hash-partition metadata to avoid hot spots. Tectonic splits metadata into name, file, and block layers and hash-partitions each one.
deeper:
Chapter 2 covers metadata services in depth; this section distills the scaling lessons. The single-server design, as in HDFS, holds all metadata in one machine's memory, which caps the number of files at what that memory can hold and makes that server a throughput bottleneck. Moving metadata into a sharded database removes both limits: capacity and throughput grow with the database's shard count.

Tectonic's layering is a clever application of partitioning.
