The name layer maps paths and directories to files, the file layer maps files to blocks, and the block layer maps blocks to storage locations. Each layer is a separate set of key-value tables, and each is hash-partitioned independently. The paper says this effectively avoids hotspots in the metadata layer.

Hash partitioning matters because metadata access is naturally skewed. A range-partitioned namespace would put a busy directory, and all its children, on one shard. Hashing spreads that load. The price is the usual one for hashing: operations that walk a directory in order or touch many related entries may need to visit several shards.

quiz.q: Why does Tectonic hash-partition each layer of its metadata?
quiz.a: Metadata access is skewed toward popular files and directories; hash partitioning spreads those hot entries across shards, which the paper says effectively avoids metadata hotspots.

title: 10.7 billion files in one cluster: size metadata for the count
body: The third metadata lesson is to count objects, not only bytes. A representative Meta Tectonic cluster in 2021 had 1,590 PB of capacity, 1,250 PB used, 10.7 billion files, and 15 billion blocks, all on 4,208 storage nodes. That is billions of metadata items in a single cluster. Whatever holds that metadata must be sized for the number of items it tracks, not for the number of petabytes, because every file and block is an entry to store, index, and look up.
deeper:
The numbers make the point concrete. Petabytes of capacity are served by a few thousand storage nodes, since each node holds many large drives. But the metadata system must track tens of billions of entries across files and blocks, and every read or write touches some of them. A metadata design sized by bytes, for example one node per few petabytes, would be hopelessly undersized for the entry count.

The same cluster snapshot appears again in the capacity planning section, as an example of a cluster kept below full: 1,250 PB used out of 1,590 PB works out to about 79 percent (the chapter rounds it to about 70 percent there).

This connects to the chapter's opening table, where object count is listed as a separate scale dimension from capacity, breaking index size, memory per object, and directory size. It is also why grouping techniques matter: Ceph tracks placement groups rather than individual objects, to keep per-item overhead manageable. When planning a storage system, ask for expected files and blocks, and size the metadata tier for that number.

quiz.q: Why must Tectonic's metadata system be sized by item count rather than by petabytes?
quiz.a: Every file and block is a metadata entry to store and look up; one cluster had 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks, far beyond what byte-based sizing implies.

title: Multi-tenancy: shared hardware, shared pain
body: A tenant is a user of the storage system with its own identity, quota, and expectations: a team, an application, or an external customer. Multi-tenancy means many tenants share the same hardware. It saves huge amounts of money, because one team's idle capacity can serve another team's peak instead of every team buying for its own worst case. But it creates the noisy neighbor problem: one tenant's burst, such as a large batch job, can hurt everyone else's latency on the shared machines.
deeper:
Multi-tenancy is the organizational version of the aggregation effect seen in S3: independent demands peak at different times, so a shared pool needs less total hardware than separate pools sized for each peak. In the running example, search, ads, and ML all share one cluster, and the savings are large.

The noisy neighbor problem is the other side of the same coin. Sharing means one tenant's resource use directly affects others: the same disks, network links, and metadata servers serve everyone. A background analytics scan can fill disk queues that a user-facing service depends on. Because the tenants have different owners and priorities, the problem is as much organizational as technical.

The chapter's answer, developed in the next cards, is a set of isolation tools, quotas, token-bucket admission control, priority classes with fair scheduling, and physical isolation for the largest tenants, plus explicit decisions about which resources are guaranteed and which are best-effort. Meta's Tectonic and Amazon DynamoDB provide the concrete examples. The senior staff lens frames it bluntly: multi-tenancy is an economic decision with a reliability cost.

quiz.q: What is the noisy neighbor problem, and why does multi-tenancy create it?
quiz.a: When tenants share hardware, one tenant's burst consumes shared disks, network, or metadata capacity and raises everyone else's latency.

title: Four tools to keep tenants from hurting each other
body: Storage systems isolate tenants with four main tools. Quotas set hard limits on bytes, objects, or request rate per tenant. Admission control with token buckets limits request rates: tokens refill at a fixed rate, each request takes one, and an empty bucket means reject or delay the request. Priority classes and fair scheduling at each storage node decide whose requests go first when resources are contended. Physical isolation, separate clusters or cells, is reserved for the biggest or most sensitive tenants.
deeper:
The tools work at different time scales and strengths. Quotas are coarse and slow-changing, suited to capacity, which Tectonic calls a non-ephemeral resource. Token buckets handle rates and allow short bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a long-run average, which is why they appear throughout the chapter: DynamoDB's global admission control is built on table-level token buckets, with partition-level buckets as defense in depth.

Priority classes and fair scheduling deal with the moment of contention on a single node. When a disk queue is full, the scheduler decides which tenant's request is served next. Without it, whoever sends the most requests wins. Tectonic's weighted round-robin scheduler with Gold, Silver, and Bronze traffic classes is the chapter's example.

Physical isolation is the strongest and most expensive tool. Separate clusters or cells eliminate interference but give up the pooling savings that motivate multi-tenancy in the first place. That is why it is reserved for tenants large enough to justify their own hardware or sensitive enough that sharing is unacceptable. Most systems combine several of these tools.

quiz.q: How does a token bucket limit a tenant's request rate?
quiz.a: Tokens refill at a fixed rate and each request consumes one; when the bucket is empty, requests are rejected or delayed, allowing short bursts but capping the average rate.

title: Tectonic: capacity is reserved, IOPS is shared
body: Meta's Tectonic (FAST 2021) divides resources into two kinds. Non-ephemeral resources, mainly storage capacity, change slowly and, once given to a tenant, cannot be shared, since bytes on disk belong to someone. These are managed with quotas. Ephemeral resources, such as storage IOPS and metadata query capacity, have demand that changes quickly, moment to moment. These must be shared dynamically, because reserving them statically would leave most of them idle while other tenants starve.
deeper:
The distinction answers a practical question: which resources should be guaranteed and which should be pooled? Capacity is naturally exclusive. If tenant A stores a petabyte, that space is taken until A deletes the data; no amount of scheduling lets tenant B use it in the meantime. So a quota, a fixed allocation that changes on planning timescales, is the right tool.

IOPS and metadata operations are the opposite. An IOPS not used this second is gone forever, and one tenant's demand may swing from zero to peak within seconds. Carving them into fixed per-tenant slices would waste most of the fleet's performance, the same waste that static sharding and DynamoDB's per-partition limits suffered from.

Tectonic's answer is to give each tenant a guaranteed quota of ephemeral resources, so every tenant can count on a baseline, and then to redistribute unused ephemeral capacity dynamically. The next card covers exactly how spare capacity flows, first within a tenant by traffic class, then to other tenants. This hybrid gives both predictability and efficiency.

quiz.q: Why does Tectonic manage storage capacity with quotas but share IOPS dynamically?
quiz.a: Capacity changes slowly and cannot be shared once used, so quotas fit; IOPS demand swings quickly and unused IOPS are lost, so they must be pooled dynamically.

title: Gold, Silver, Bronze: Tectonic's traffic classes
body: Inside each Tectonic tenant, applications are grouped into about 50 TrafficGroups per cluster, and each TrafficGroup has a TrafficClass: Gold for latency-sensitive, Silver for normal, and Bronze for background work. Each tenant gets a guaranteed quota of ephemeral resources such as IOPS. Spare capacity flows first to the tenant's own TrafficGroups by class, then to other tenants. Storage nodes run a weighted round-robin scheduler that skips a TrafficGroup's turn if it would exceed its limit, and lets lower-class requests yield to Gold requests.
deeper:
TrafficGroups give Tectonic a manageable unit of isolation. Instead of tracking many individual applications separately, it tracks about 50 groups per cluster, each with a class that encodes how urgent its requests are.

The spare-capacity order reflects ownership and priority. A tenant's unused guarantee benefits its own groups first, in class order, so its Gold work is covered before its Bronze. Only then does leftover capacity flow to other tenants. This rewards tenants for their guarantee while still keeping the fleet busy.

On each storage node, weighted round-robin serves groups in turn according to their weights, but skips a group whose next request would push it over its limit, so a greedy group cannot monopolize the disk. The yielding optimization lets a Bronze or Silver request step aside when a Gold request is waiting, protecting latency-sensitive traffic.

This design is also a tail-latency tool: the chapter recommends scheduling background work, such as compaction and repair, at lower priority, as Tectonic's TrafficClasses do. The key takeaways summarize it: multi-tenancy needs guaranteed quotas plus priority classes for shared, ephemeral resources.

quiz.q: How does Tectonic's scheduler protect Gold traffic on a busy storage node?
quiz.a: Weighted round-robin skips any TrafficGroup that would exceed its limit, and lower-class requests yield to waiting Gold requests, so latency-sensitive work goes first.

title: Shared clusters paid off: 10x fewer warehouse clusters
body: Tectonic's isolation design made consolidation possible. By moving blob storage and the data warehouse onto shared Tectonic clusters, Meta reduced the number of data warehouse clusters by 10x, and the warehouse could absorb traffic spikes using blob storage's spare IOPS. DynamoDB faces the same challenge in a public service: storage nodes host thousands of replicas from unrelated customers, so it caps partition-level token buckets to ensure one application does not consume all or a significant share of a node's resources.
deeper:
The Tectonic result shows why the isolation machinery is worth building. Blob storage and the data warehouse have complementary profiles: blob storage holds huge volumes of data with IOPS to spare, while warehouse workloads are spiky. Once they share clusters with guaranteed quotas and traffic classes, the warehouse's spikes are absorbed by capacity that would otherwise sit idle in blob storage. Meta reported a 10x reduction in warehouse clusters.

DynamoDB shows the same tension in a harder setting. Meta's tenants are internal teams that can be negotiated with; DynamoDB's tenants are external customers who never see each other and expect predictable performance. Global admission control gives each customer flexibility across its own partitions, but the partition-level token bucket cap exists specifically so that one customer's hot partition cannot take over a storage node shared with thousands of other customers' replicas.

In both cases, the savings of sharing depend on enforcement. Without quotas, scheduling, and caps, consolidation would turn into constant noisy-neighbor incidents rather than a 10x efficiency gain.

quiz.q: Why does DynamoDB keep partition-level token bucket caps even with table-level admission control?
quiz.a: Storage nodes host thousands of replicas from unrelated customers, so caps stop one application's hot partition from consuming all or a large share of a node's resources.

title: Senior staff lens: multi-tenancy is economics with a reliability bill
body: Multi-tenancy is an economic decision with a reliability cost. Before sharing a cluster, ask: What is the isolation unit, the tenant, the application, or the request class? Which resources are guaranteed and which are best-effort? What happens to a Gold request when the cluster is full of Bronze work? Who pays for headroom? If nobody can answer these questions, the shared cluster will become a political problem the first time a batch job hurts a user-facing service.
deeper:
This lens reframes multi-tenancy from a technical feature to an agreement between teams. The savings are real, as Tectonic's 10x consolidation shows, but they come from people sharing resources they would otherwise control alone. When something goes wrong, the questions become who caused it, whose work should have been protected, and who should have paid to prevent it.

Each question maps to a design decision earlier in the chapter. The isolation unit is what Tectonic's TrafficGroups and DynamoDB's tables and partitions define. Guaranteed versus best-effort is Tectonic's split between guaranteed ephemeral quotas and redistributed spare capacity. The Gold-versus-Bronze question is about scheduling and preemption, answered by weighted round-robin with yielding. Headroom is about budget: someone must fund spare capacity so that bursts and repairs do not hurt guaranteed tenants.

The warning at the end is practical. Without written answers, the first incident where a batch job slows a user-facing service turns into an argument about blame and priority rather than a quick application of agreed policy.

quiz.q: What happens if a shared storage cluster has no agreed answers about isolation units and guarantees?
quiz.a: The first time a batch job hurts a user-facing service, it becomes a political fight over blame and priority instead of applying an agreed policy.

title: 70 to 80 ms: the speed-of-light floor for global writes
body: A 1-billion-user app has users on every continent. Light in fiber needs roughly 70 to 80 ms for a round trip between the US East Coast and Western Europe, using typical published figures. A strongly consistent write that must reach a quorum spread across continents cannot complete faster than that, no matter how good the software is. This physical limit shapes every multi-region design: each one decides which operations pay the cross-region round trip and which stay local.
deeper:
The number is a floor, not an estimate of real latency. Actual round trips include routing, queuing, and processing, so they are higher. Consensus protocols may also need more than one round trip per write. The key point is that software cannot beat physics: if a write must be acknowledged by replicas on two continents, it will take at least one intercontinental round trip.

The rest of the section is a toolbox for living with this limit. Asynchronous replication keeps writes local and pays for it with possible data loss and conflicts. Synchronous replication pays the round trip in exchange for no data loss and strong consistency. Leader placement puts the write-ordering replica close to the writers so most writes stay fast. Akkio-style migration moves data to follow its users. Conflict resolution techniques, such as last-writer-wins, vector clocks, and CRDTs, handle concurrent writes in async designs, and home regions avoid conflicts altogether.

Data residency laws add a legal constraint on top of physics: some data cannot simply be placed wherever latency is best.

quiz.q: Why can't a strongly consistent cross-continent write be faster than about 70 to 80 ms?
quiz.a: It must reach a quorum spread across continents, and light in fiber needs roughly 70 to 80 ms for a US East to Western Europe round trip.

title: Sync vs async replication: pay in latency or in lost writes
body: Synchronous replication acknowledges a write only after a quorum in multiple regions has it. Writes pay a cross-region round trip, but a region failure loses no data (RPO = 0) and strong consistency is possible. Examples: Spanner multi-region and Physalia-style designs. Asynchronous replication acknowledges once the local region has the write, so latency is local only, but recent writes can be lost if the region fails, and consistency is eventual with possible conflicts. Examples: DynamoDB global tables, Cassandra multi-DC with local quorum, most blob geo-replication.
deeper:
Two terms frame the trade-off. RPO, recovery point objective, is how much recent data you can afford to lose. RTO, recovery time objective, is how long you can afford to be down. Synchronous replication achieves RPO = 0 because no write is acknowledged until it exists in several regions. Asynchronous replication has a nonzero RPO: writes acknowledged locally but not yet shipped are lost if that region disappears.

Consistency follows the same split. With synchronous quorums, a read can be guaranteed to see the latest write. With asynchronous replication, other regions lag behind, and if two regions accept writes to the same item concurrently, the system must resolve conflicts later.

The chapter's key takeaway puts it simply: multi-region design is a choice between write latency and data loss. Many real systems mix both, using synchronous replication for critical metadata or small, important records, and asynchronous replication for bulk data like photos and logs, where a few seconds of possible loss or staleness is acceptable in exchange for local write speed.

quiz.q: What is the core trade-off between synchronous and asynchronous multi-region replication?
quiz.a: Synchronous pays a cross-region round trip per write but loses nothing on region failure (RPO = 0); asynchronous keeps writes local but can lose recent writes and allows conflicts.

title: Spanner: put writers next to the default leader region
body: Many strongly consistent systems have a leader per shard that orders writes, and where that leader lives decides write latency. Google Spanner makes this explicit. A regional configuration has three read-write replicas in different zones of one region. Multi-region configurations spread read-write replicas across regions, plus a witness region that votes but holds no full data copy. Each configuration has a default leader region that handles writes, and Google advises placing compute for write-heavy workloads within or close to that region.
deeper:
The advice follows from the physics. Every write goes through the shard's leader, so a writer far from the leader pays a long round trip on every write before consensus even starts. Placing application servers in or near the default leader region keeps that hop short.

The witness region is an economical way to get a majority vote across regions without paying for another full copy of the data. It participates in consensus, helping the system tolerate a regional failure, but does not store all the data.

Google describes the multi-region trade-off as faster reads in more places at the cost of a small increase in write latency. Reads can be served by nearby replicas, while writes need agreement across regions.

Spanner also offers dual-region configurations that keep all replicas inside one country, which exist for data residency: they allow regional failure tolerance and failover without data leaving the permitted jurisdiction. This connects leader placement to the legal constraints covered later in the section.

quiz.q: Why does Google advise placing write-heavy compute near Spanner's default leader region?
quiz.a: Every write is ordered by the shard's leader, so a writer far from the leader region adds a long round trip to every write.

title: Akkio: move each user's data to where they are
body: Rather than fixing a leader region, a smarter approach moves leaders, or whole data, to where they are used. Meta's Akkio (OSDI 2018) groups related data into u-shards, for example all of one user's data, and migrates them between datacenters to follow access patterns. If a user starts accessing from a different region, their data moves closer. The paper reports up to 50 percent lower access latency, up to 50 percent less cross-datacenter traffic, and up to 40 percent less storage, managing over 100 PB in production.
deeper:
Akkio's insight is that the right unit for locality is not the database shard but a group of data that is accessed together. A u-shard, such as one user's data, is small enough to move cheaply and coherent enough that moving it brings all related accesses local. Database shards, by contrast, contain many unrelated users with different locations, so no single placement suits all of them.

The paper compares Akkio with what it calls reasonable alternatives. Intuitively, lower latency comes from serving users from a nearby datacenter, less cross-datacenter traffic comes from not fetching remote data on every access, and less storage comes from not needing a full copy of every user's data in every location.

The approach fits the chapter's broader theme that directory-style, movable placement beats fixed hash-based placement at scale. Meta's Shard Manager paper similarly found that most applications need geo-distribution, so placement must span regions. Akkio also complements the home-region idea in conflict resolution: a user's data has a home, and that home can move with the user.

quiz.q: What is Akkio's u-shard, and why migrate it instead of whole database shards?
quiz.a: A u-shard groups related data, such as one user's; moving it follows that user's access, whereas database shards mix users in many locations.

title: Last-writer-wins: simple, popular, and silently lossy
body: With asynchronous multi-region writes, two regions can update the same item at the same time, and the system must choose a result. Last-writer-wins (LWW) attaches a timestamp to each write and keeps the latest. It is simple and widely used, for example in Cassandra's per-column timestamps and DynamoDB global tables. The costs: with clock skew between machines, a write that truly happened later can carry an earlier timestamp and silently lose. And if the unit is a whole item, concurrent updates to different fields overwrite each other.
deeper:
LWW's appeal is that it needs no coordination and no application logic: every replica applies the same rule and converges on the same value. That is why it is the default in many eventually consistent systems.

The first cost comes from clocks. Different machines' clocks drift, so timestamps from two regions are not perfectly comparable. If region A's clock runs slightly fast, its writes win even when region B wrote afterward. The losing write simply disappears with no error, which makes these bugs hard to notice.

The second cost is granularity. If a user updates their display name in one region while updating their photo in another, and the system treats the whole profile as one unit, one of those changes is lost even though they touched different fields. Cassandra reduces this by keeping timestamps per column, so concurrent updates to different columns both survive.

LWW works well when overwrites are acceptable, such as a latest-status field, and poorly when every write matters, such as counters or carts, where the other techniques in this section are better choices.

quiz.q: How can last-writer-wins silently lose a write that really happened later?
quiz.a: Clock skew can give the later write an earlier timestamp, so the replicas keep the other write and discard it without any error.

title: Vector clocks: keep both versions, let the app merge
body: The Dynamo paper (2007) took a different approach to conflicts: use vector clocks to detect when two versions were written concurrently, keep both conflicting versions, and let the application merge them. The classic example is a shopping cart: if two regions each added an item to the same cart, the application merges both carts so neither item is lost. This is powerful, because no write is silently discarded, but it pushes complexity onto developers, who must write correct merge logic for every data type.
deeper:
A vector clock tracks, per replica, how many updates each version has seen. Comparing two vector clocks tells the system whether one version descends from the other, in which case the newer one simply replaces it, or whether they were written independently, in which case they are true conflicts. Unlike LWW timestamps, this does not depend on synchronized wall clocks.

When a true conflict exists, Dynamo does not guess. It returns both versions to the application on the next read, and the application decides how to combine them. For a shopping cart, taking the union of items is a sensible merge, though it can bring back an item a user deleted in one region.

The cost is that every application must handle conflicts correctly, for every kind of data it stores, and bugs in merge logic can corrupt data. That burden is one reason many later systems chose simpler LWW semantics, or moved to CRDTs, which bake a well-defined merge into the data type itself, or avoided conflicts entirely with single-writer home regions.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off of Dynamo's approach of keeping conflicting versions for the app to merge?
quiz.a: No write is silently lost, but every application must implement correct merge logic for its data, pushing significant complexity onto developers.

title: CRDTs: data types that always merge cleanly
body: CRDTs, Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, are data types designed so that merging replicas is always well-defined and all replicas converge to the same value, no matter the order in which updates arrive. Examples include counters, sets, maps, and registers. They are a good fit for likes counters, presence indicators, and collaborative editing, where many regions update concurrently. The limit: not every business rule can be expressed as a CRDT. A rule like balance must not go below zero needs coordination.
deeper:
CRDTs move merge logic from the application into the data type. A counter CRDT, for example, can track increments per region and sum them, so concurrent increments in different regions never overwrite each other and every replica eventually reports the same total. Because the merge is mathematically guaranteed to converge, replicas can accept writes locally with no coordination and still agree once updates propagate.

This makes CRDTs attractive for the running example's social features: likes, view counts, online-presence flags, and collaborative documents all involve many concurrent writers and tolerate brief disagreement between regions.

The boundary is invariants that depend on the global state. A bank balance that must never go negative cannot be enforced by independent local decisions: two regions could each approve a withdrawal that is valid locally, and together overdraw the account. Enforcing that rule requires coordination, such as a single owner or a synchronous consensus step, which reintroduces the cross-region latency CRDTs were meant to avoid. So CRDTs are a tool for the right data, not a universal answer to multi-region consistency.

quiz.q: Why can't a rule like “balance must not go below zero” be handled by a CRDT?
quiz.a: It is a global invariant: regions deciding independently could each approve valid-looking withdrawals that together overdraw, so enforcing it needs coordination.

title: Home regions: avoid conflicts by giving each item one writer
body: The simplest way to handle conflicts is to avoid them by design. Give each item a home region that owns all writes to it, a single writer per key, and replicate asynchronously to other regions for reads. Because only one region ever accepts writes for a given item, two regions can never update it concurrently, so there is nothing to resolve. This is very common for user data: your profile is written in your home region and read from replicas elsewhere.
deeper:
Home regions trade some write latency for simplicity. A user who travels far from their home region pays a cross-region round trip on writes, since those writes must go home. Reads remain fast everywhere because asynchronous replicas serve them locally, though they may be slightly stale.

For most user data this is an excellent trade. Users mostly stay near their home, their data is mostly written by themselves, and slightly stale reads by others are acceptable. The design needs a router that knows each user's home region; the chapter's residency diagram shows exactly that: an EU user's profile write goes to a router that reads the user's home region and sends the write to the EU leader region.

Home regions combine naturally with other ideas in the section. Akkio shows the home can move when a user relocates, keeping writes local. Data residency rules can be enforced by choosing the home region according to jurisdiction. And because writes are ordered in one place, the application gets predictable semantics without the clock-skew risk of LWW or the merge complexity of vector clocks.

quiz.q: How does a home region per item avoid write conflicts?
quiz.a: Only the home region accepts writes for that item, so there is a single writer per key and concurrent cross-region updates never happen; other regions get async read replicas.

title: Data residency is a placement constraint, not a policy doc
body: Data residency laws, such as rules in the EU, India, or China, may require certain data to be stored or processed inside a country or region. In a storage system this becomes a hard placement constraint. The shard manager or placement layer must know each shard's jurisdiction and refuse illegal placements. Backups, logs, caches, and analytics copies are also copies and must follow the same rule. Failover targets must be inside the allowed area, which is why Spanner's dual-region configurations keep all replicas within one country.
deeper:
The chapter's diagram traces an EU user's profile write under a placement policy of residency = EU. The router reads the user's home region and sends the write to the EU leader region. From there, a synchronous quorum replicates inside EU zones, backups are stored in the EU only, and a US read replica receives an asynchronous stream containing allowed fields only. That last detail shows residency can be field-level: some parts of a record may leave the region while personal data does not.

Making residency a placement constraint means encoding it where placement decisions are made. Shard managers like Meta's already let applications declare constraints such as keep a shard near its users; jurisdiction is another constraint of the same kind, but one that must never be violated for load or cost reasons.

Failover is the easy thing to forget. A disaster recovery plan that fails EU data over to a US region breaks the law at exactly the moment everyone is busy. Spanner's dual-region configurations exist so that a customer can tolerate the loss of a region without data leaving the country.

quiz.q: Why must data residency be enforced in the placement layer rather than only in policy?
quiz.a: Placement decides where every copy and failover target lives; only there can illegal placements be refused automatically, including backups, logs, caches, and analytics copies.

title: Common mistake: residency enforced only in the primary database
body: A common mistake is enforcing data residency only in the primary database. The main tables stay in the EU, but a debug log, an analytics export, or a cross-region backup quietly copies personal data abroad. Every one of those is a copy, and the law applies to copies. Residency must be treated as a property of the data itself, carried along with it and enforced on every copy path, not as a setting on one database.
deeper:
Copies multiply in a large system. Application logs capture request payloads. Analytics pipelines export tables to a central warehouse, often in one region. Caches sit in edge locations worldwide. Backups are often sent to a distant region for disaster recovery. Cross-region read replicas serve users elsewhere. Failover replicas are prepared in case of regional outage. Each of these paths can move EU personal data out of the EU without anyone touching the primary database.

The chapter's check-your-understanding answer lists backups, logs, caches, analytics exports, failover replicas, and cross-region read replicas as copy paths that must follow the rule.

Treating residency as a property of the data means tagging data with its jurisdiction and having every pipeline, backup job, cache, and replication stream respect that tag. The diagram in the residency section shows one piece of this: the asynchronous stream to a US read replica carries allowed fields only, and backups are stored in the EU only. Audits should trace every path data can take, not just where the primary copy sits.

quiz.q: Your EU user data must stay in the EU. Name three copy paths besides the primary database that must follow the rule.
quiz.a: Any three of: backups, logs, caches, analytics exports, failover replicas, and cross-region read replicas.

title: Capacity planning: buy it months before you need it
body: Capacity planning means predicting how much storage, IOPS, network, and power you will need, and buying it before you need it. It is hard for two reasons. Lead times are long: servers must be purchased, shipped, racked, and burned in, and new datacenter space needs power and cooling built. In general industry experience, server lead times are months and new buildings take years. And demand is lumpy: a product launch or a new ML dataset can add petabytes in weeks, while data rarely shrinks.
deeper:
The combination is what makes planning risky. If demand were smooth and hardware could be delivered in days, you could simply buy as you go. Instead, you must commit money months or years ahead based on a forecast, and the forecast can be wrong in either direction. Underbuy and you run out of room; overbuy and expensive hardware sits idle.

The chapter notes that exact lead times are rarely published, so it speaks in general terms: months for servers, years for buildings. Burn-in, running new hardware under load before trusting it with data, adds time even after the machines arrive.

Lumpiness makes forecasting harder than a simple trend line. A single new ML training dataset or a feature launch that stores video can add petabytes quickly. And because data rarely shrinks, every spike becomes a permanent step up in the baseline. Planning must account for both the steady trend and the likelihood of sudden jumps, which is why the basic model includes a safety buffer for forecast error on top of expected growth.

quiz.q: What two factors make storage capacity planning hard at hyperscale?
quiz.a: Long lead times (months for servers, years for buildings) and lumpy demand, where launches or new datasets add petabytes in weeks and data rarely shrinks.

title: 100 PB growing 3 percent a month needs 149 PB in 6 months
body: The chapter's teaching model, with all numbers assumed: current usage is 100 PB, growth is 3 percent per month, and hardware lead time is 6 months. In 6 months, usage will be about 100 x 1.03^6, roughly 119 PB. With a target maximum fill of 80 percent, you need about 119 / 0.8, roughly 149 PB of raw usable capacity installed by then. On top of that, add a safety buffer for forecast error, such as another month or two of growth.
deeper:
Each step in the model represents a real planning concern. Compounding growth over the lead time answers how much data you will have when the hardware you order today finally arrives. Growth compounds, so 3 percent per month over 6 months is about 19 percent, not 18.

Dividing by the target fill converts expected usage into required capacity. The 80 percent target reserves free space for repair, rebalancing, and bursts, as the next card explains. Without that division you would plan to be 100 percent full, which in distributed storage is dangerous.

The safety buffer handles the lumpy demand problem. Forecasts are wrong, and the cost of being short is much higher than the cost of a little extra hardware, so planners add another month or two of growth.

Notice what the model outputs: a target for installed capacity at a future date. Combined with the lead time, that tells you when to place the order. The senior staff lens later turns this into a policy question about which fill levels trigger an order and which trigger an incident.

quiz.q: In the basic capacity model, why divide projected usage by 0.8?
quiz.a: The target maximum fill is 80 percent, leaving free space for repair, rebalancing, and bursts, so installed capacity must be projected usage divided by 0.8.

title: Never run distributed storage full: repair needs room
body: Distributed storage must never run full. When a disk or rack fails, its data must be re-created somewhere else from the remaining replicas or erasure-coded fragments, and that requires free space on other machines. If the cluster is 95 percent full, there may be no room to repair, and an ordinary hardware failure turns into real data risk, because the lost redundancy cannot be restored. That is why capacity models target a maximum fill such as 80 percent. The chapter cites Meta's Tectonic representative 2021 cluster as about 70 percent full.
deeper:
Free space is part of the durability design, not waste. Replication and erasure coding protect data only if lost copies are quickly rebuilt. A full cluster breaks that loop: after a failure, data sits with reduced redundancy, and a second failure during that window can cause loss.

Free space also serves the other background processes the chapter describes. Rebalancing needs room on destination servers to receive shards. Continuous add-and-retire needs room to drain racks before powering them off, since every chunk from the retiring rack must land elsewhere with full redundancy. Bursts of new data need room too.

The Tectonic snapshot shows a real operator keeping headroom: the chapter calls it about 70 percent full, though its own figures, 1,250 PB used of 1,590 PB, work out to roughly 79 percent, just under the 80 percent target. The chapter's key takeaway puts it bluntly: never run storage near full, and plan capacity with lead time, growth, buffer, and repair headroom. The senior staff lens that follows turns this into an operational policy, distinguishing the fill level that triggers a hardware order from the fill level that triggers an incident.

quiz.q: Why is a 95 percent full distributed storage cluster dangerous even if nothing has failed yet?
quiz.a: When a disk or rack fails, its data must be rebuilt elsewhere; with little free space there may be no room to restore redundancy, so a routine failure becomes data risk.

title: No big-bang upgrades: racks arrive and leave every week
body: Big storage fleets never upgrade in one step. Every week new racks arrive and old racks retire. This works only under three conditions. The placement layer must support heterogeneous hardware, such as disks of different sizes weighted by capacity, as CRUSH weights do. New capacity must be filled gradually through rate-limited rebalancing. And old capacity must be drained before removal: mark the rack as draining, move its data out, verify every chunk has full redundancy elsewhere, then power off.
deeper:
Heterogeneity is unavoidable in a fleet that adds and removes hardware continuously. At any moment, several generations of disks and servers coexist, with different capacities and performance. A placement system that assumes identical machines would overfill small disks and underuse big ones. Weighting, as in CRUSH's cluster map or vnode counts in consistent hashing, lets each device receive a share proportional to its capacity.

Gradual filling is the lesson from the rebalancing common mistake: an empty new rack attracts a flood of data from a naive balancer, which can saturate the network for hours. Rate limits keep that migration in the background.

Draining is the safety-critical step. Simply unplugging an old rack would remove copies and reduce redundancy for every chunk it held, effectively simulating a large failure. Instead, the rack is marked draining so no new data lands there, its data is copied out, and the system verifies that every chunk has full redundancy elsewhere before anyone powers it off. Chapter 9 covers the operational side of decommissioning.

quiz.q: Why must a retiring rack be drained and verified before it is powered off?
quiz.a: Powering it off directly removes copies and reduces redundancy like a failure would; draining moves data out and confirms every chunk is fully redundant elsewhere first.

title: Senior staff lens: the gap between order and incident
body: Capacity planning is where storage engineering meets finance. A useful review question is: what fill level triggers a hardware order, and what fill level triggers an incident? The gap between those two levels must be larger than the hardware lead time multiplied by the worst realistic growth rate. If it is smaller, then by the time an order is placed, demand can reach the incident level before the new hardware arrives, and the team will be in crisis with nothing to deploy.
deeper:
This question turns the capacity model into an operational policy. The order threshold is when the team commits money. The incident threshold is the fill level at which repair headroom is at risk, and people should be paged. Between them lies the runway.

The runway must cover lead time multiplied by the worst realistic growth rate, not the average. For example, in the chapter's model, 6 months of lead time at 3 percent monthly growth adds about 19 percent more data. If growth could plausibly jump because of a launch or a new ML dataset, the gap must cover that faster rate. Otherwise a lumpy month consumes the runway before the new racks are racked and burned in.

The finance connection is that a wider gap means buying earlier and carrying more idle hardware, which costs money, while a narrower gap saves money but risks running out. Making the trade-off explicit, with both thresholds written down and tied to lead time and growth, lets engineering and finance agree on the risk they are taking instead of discovering it during an outage.

quiz.q: How large must the gap be between the fill level that triggers an order and the one that triggers an incident?
quiz.a: Larger than hardware lead time multiplied by the worst realistic growth rate, so demand cannot hit the incident level before new capacity arrives.

title: Fan out to 100 servers and 63 percent of requests are slow
body: When one user request touches many servers, the slowest server decides the latency. Jeff Dean and Luiz Barroso's The Tail at Scale (CACM 2013) gives the classic example. Suppose a server usually answers in 10 ms, but 1 request in 100 takes 1 second. If a user request touches one server, 1 in 100 is slow. If it must wait for 100 such servers in parallel, the chance all 100 are fast is 0.99^100, about 0.37. So about 63 percent of user requests take over a second.
deeper:
The math is the probability of avoiding every slow response. Each server independently has a 99 percent chance of being fast, so for N servers the chance all are fast is 0.99 to the power N. At 100 servers that is about 37 percent, meaning a rare per-server event becomes the common case for the user. The chapter's quiz applies the same formula to 50 servers: 1 minus 0.99^50 is about 0.39, so about 39 percent of requests are slow.

The tail has several sources in storage systems. Background work such as compaction, scrubbing, and rebalancing temporarily slows servers. Noisy neighbors in multi-tenant clusters consume shared resources. Queueing adds delay when requests arrive in bursts. Slowly failing hardware, such as a disk that still works but responds slowly, can drag down every request that touches it.

Fan-out is common in the chapter's designs: hash-partitioned range queries scatter to every shard, salted counters read N sub-keys, and erasure-coded reads fetch many fragments. Each of these multiplies exposure to the tail, which is why tail latency techniques matter at scale.

quiz.q: A request fans out to 50 servers, each 1 percent likely to be slow. Roughly what fraction of requests are slow?
quiz.a: 1 minus 0.99^50, about 0.39, so roughly 39 percent. Try hedged requests after a p95 delay first, and look for the root cause of the slow tail.

title: Hedged requests: 1,800 ms to 74 ms for 2 percent more load
body: A hedged request sends a request to one replica, and if no reply arrives after a short delay, for example the 95th percentile latency, sends a second copy to another replica and uses whichever answers first. Most requests finish before the hedge fires, so extra load stays small. In a Google benchmark reading 1,000 keys from Bigtable across 100 servers, hedging after 10 ms cut 99.9th percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms, while sending only 2 percent more requests.
deeper:
The chapter's sequence diagram shows the flow. The client sends GET key to Replica A and waits about 10 ms, the p95 delay. No answer has arrived, so it sends a hedge GET key to Replica B. Replica B returns the value quickly, and the client cancels the outstanding request to Replica A.

The delay is what makes hedging cheap. By waiting until the 95th percentile, the client hedges only the roughly 5 percent of requests that are already slow, and many of those are stuck behind a temporary problem on one replica, such as compaction or a noisy neighbor. A second replica is unlikely to be slow at the same moment, so the hedge usually wins.

The benchmark numbers illustrate the leverage: a dramatic cut in extreme tail latency, from 1,800 ms to 74 ms at the 99.9th percentile, for only 2 percent extra requests. The chapter's quiz answer recommends hedged requests after a p95 delay as the first technique to try for a fan-out tail problem, while also investigating the root cause of the slow tail.

quiz.q: Why wait until about the 95th percentile before sending a hedged request?
quiz.a: Most requests finish by then, so only the slow few get duplicated; the hedge rescues stragglers while adding only a few percent extra load.

title: Tied requests: two queues, one cancels the other
body: A tied request sends the same request to two servers at once, and each copy knows about the other. When one server actually starts executing the request, it tells the other server to cancel its copy. The goal is to avoid waiting in a long queue: whichever server reaches the request first does the work, and the other drops it before spending effort. This attacks tail latency caused by queueing, where a request's delay comes from waiting behind others rather than from its own processing time.
deeper:
Tied requests address a weakness of hedging. A hedge waits for a delay before sending the second copy, so a request stuck in a long queue still loses that waiting time. A tied request enqueues on both servers immediately, so it gets the shorter of the two queue waits without any delay.

The cancellation message is what keeps the cost down. Without it, sending every request to two servers would double the load, which is exactly the problem the chapter warns about with immediate hedging. Because the servers coordinate, only one of them performs the actual work in the common case; the other copy is removed from its queue once execution starts elsewhere. There is a small window in which both might start at nearly the same moment, but the extra work is limited.

Queueing is a major source of tail latency in storage systems, since requests arrive in bursts and background work can occupy a server. Tied requests let the client benefit from whichever server happens to be less busy at that moment, without predicting it in advance.

quiz.q: How do tied requests avoid doubling server load despite sending every request twice?
quiz.a: Each copy knows about the other; when one server starts executing, it tells the other to cancel, so usually only one server does the work.

title: Ask for 12 fragments, decode from the first 10
body: Two more tail-latency techniques fit storage well. Erasure-code read slack: with a Reed-Solomon RS(10,4) stripe, any 10 of the 14 fragments can rebuild the data, so a reader can request 11 or 12 fragments and decode from the first 10 that arrive, simply ignoring slow disks. Separating background work: schedule compaction, repair, and similar maintenance at lower priority than user requests, as Tectonic's TrafficClasses do, so it does not create the slow responses in the first place.
deeper:
Read slack takes advantage of redundancy that already exists for durability. A plain RS(10,4) read would fetch exactly 10 fragments and be as slow as the slowest of those 10 disks, a fan-out of 10 with full exposure to the tail. Requesting one or two extra fragments means the read completes when the 10 fastest responses arrive, and a disk that is busy, compacting, or failing slowly is skipped automatically. The cost is modestly more read traffic.

Separating background work tackles a root cause. The chapter lists background work such as compaction, scrubbing, and rebalancing as a named source of the tail. Running it at the same priority as user traffic guarantees that user requests sometimes queue behind it. Tectonic's Bronze class for background work, with lower-class requests yielding to Gold requests, keeps maintenance from pushing up latency-sensitive traffic.

Together with hedged and tied requests, these form the chapter's toolkit. The key takeaway sums it up: at high fan-out, the tail decides latency, and hedged and tied requests cut tail latency with small extra load.

quiz.q: How does requesting 11 or 12 fragments of an RS(10,4) stripe reduce tail latency?
quiz.a: Any 10 fragments can decode the data, so the reader uses the first 10 to arrive and ignores slow disks instead of waiting for the slowest of exactly 10.

title: Common mistake: hedging immediately
body: A common mistake is hedging immediately, sending the duplicate request at the same time as the original. That doubles the load on the storage system, and higher load means longer queues, which makes the tail latency you were trying to fix even worse. The correct approach is to hedge only after a delay near the 95th percentile latency, so only the slow few requests get a second copy, and to cap the hedge rate so hedges cannot flood the system during a broad slowdown.
deeper:
Hedging works because slow responses are usually caused by temporary, local problems on one replica. Waiting until the 95th percentile means you duplicate only the requests that are genuinely stuck, which is why the Google Bigtable benchmark saw only 2 percent more requests while cutting 99.9th percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms.

Immediate hedging throws that away. Every request now costs two server operations, so the system needs twice the capacity to stay at the same utilization. If it does not have that capacity, queues grow, every server slows down, and the tail gets longer for everyone, the opposite of the intended effect.

The hedge-rate cap protects against a different failure. If the whole cluster slows down, for example during a large rebalance or a partial outage, many requests exceed the p95 delay at once and hedging would fire for all of them, adding load exactly when the system is weakest. A cap limits hedges to a small fraction of traffic so the mechanism cannot amplify an incident. Tied requests are the alternative when queueing is the main problem.

quiz.q: Why is sending a hedge request immediately worse than waiting for a p95 delay?
quiz.a: Immediate hedging doubles load, lengthening queues and worsening the tail; a p95 delay duplicates only the slow few, and a rate cap prevents hedge floods.

title: Chapter 8 in ten lines: split, place, stay fast
body: Scale has at least six dimensions: bytes, IOPS, metadata operations, object count, tenants, and regions, and each breaks a different component. Range partitioning keeps scans cheap but hot-spots on sequential keys; hashing spreads load but loses scans; consistent hashing with vnodes moves only about 1/N of data. Big companies converged on central shard managers. Placement spreads copies across failure domains. Multi-tenancy needs quotas plus priority classes. Multi-region design trades write latency against data loss. Never run storage near full. At high fan-out, the tail decides latency.
deeper:
The chapter's key takeaways fill in the rest. Slicer, Shard Manager, and Helix won out because operators need to place shards by load, fault domain, hardware, and region, and to drain servers before planned events. CRUSH computes placement from a cluster map and rules, while directory placement is more flexible and can be heat-aware. At huge scale, spreading each tenant over very many drives makes bursts cancel out, as in S3's heat management; small systems need explicit headroom instead.

DynamoDB's evolution shows that per-partition limits cause throttling under skew; table-level admission control plus split-for-consumption fixes most skew, but not a single hot key, which needs caching, replicas, coalescing, or salting. Tectonic's Gold, Silver, and Bronze TrafficClasses show how guaranteed quotas and priority scheduling share ephemeral resources like IOPS. For multi-region, leader placement, home regions, LWW, CRDTs, and residency constraints are the main tools, and residency must follow every copy. Capacity plans must combine lead time, growth, buffer, and repair headroom. Hedged and tied requests cut tail latency with small extra load.

quiz.q: Why did large companies converge on central, directory-style shard managers?
quiz.a: They need to place shards by load, fault domain, hardware, and region, and to drain servers gracefully before planned events, which hash-based placement cannot express.
